notes: Source claim: crawling starts from a seed set, repeatedly fetches a URL, parses text and links, passes text to the indexer, filters and normalizes extracted links into a URL frontier, and in continuous crawling returns fetched URLs to the frontier for refetching (lines 79-99).

Source claim: must-provide features are robustness against spider traps and politeness toward servers; should-provide features are distribution, scalability, performance and efficiency, quality bias toward useful pages, freshness and extensibility (lines 30-76).

Source claim: any non-professional crawler should keep one connection open per host, wait a few seconds between successive requests to a host, and obey the politeness restrictions of Section 20.2.1 (lines 110-119).

Source claim: the architecture comprises the URL frontier, DNS resolution, fetch, parsing and duplicate elimination, plus a housekeeping thread that logs crawl statistics, decides termination and checkpoints crawler state to disk every few hours (lines 124-278).

Source claim: robots.txt filtering must run immediately before fetching because a URL can wait days or weeks in the frontier, although a host-level robots.txt cache still produces high hit rates (lines 212-245).

Source claim: DNS is a known bottleneck because resolution may take seconds and standard library lookups are synchronous; the Mercator design uses a separate DNS thread on port 53, timed waits, about five retries and exponential backoff from one second to roughly 90 seconds (lines 363-409).

Source claim: the frontier separates prioritization (F front queues keyed on change rate and quality) from politeness (B back queues, one host each), with a heap of earliest permitted contact times and a new te of about now plus ten times the last fetch time; Mercator recommends roughly three back queues per crawler thread (lines 426-579).

Source claim: distribution partitions hosts through a host splitter, but document fingerprints cannot be partitioned by host, so content-seen tests become remote procedure calls with little cache locality, and fingerprints must be stored in the frontier to be deleted when documents change (lines 280-355).

Source claim: index distribution contrasts term (global) and document (local) partitioning, argues document partitioning is the more common implementation, notes that global statistics such as idf must be refreshed by background processes, and warns that host-based document assignment concentrates results on few nodes (lines 613-670).

Source claim: a connectivity server stores URL-to-out-link and URL-to-in-link tables ordered lexicographically, encodes each row against up to seven preceding prototype rows with 3-bit offsets and gap encoding, and is reported to need as few as 3 bits per link against 64 in the naive representation (lines 673-825).

Inference, not source claim: the treatment is design guidance derived from the Mercator crawler and reports no measurements of its own; the 3-bits-per-link and fetch-rate figures are attributed to cited experiments rather than reproduced here (lines 104-109, 782-784, 860-863).

notes: Source claim: link analysis borrows from citation analysis and bibliometrics, treating a hyperlink as a conferral of authority and anchor text as a description of the target, while noting that template links inside a site are not endorsements and are typically discounted (lines 12-59).

Source claim: anchor text can be indexed as terms for the target page, weighted with an idf-like penalty for very common anchors such as click and here, and extended anchor-text windows are usable; orchestrated anchor text is described as a spam vector (lines 99-133).

Source claim: PageRank is the steady-state visit frequency of a random surfer that follows an out-link with probability 1-alpha and teleports uniformly at random with probability alpha, where alpha is typically about 0.1 (lines 183-222).

Source claim: the transition matrix is derived from the adjacency matrix by replacing empty rows with 1/N, dividing each 1 by its row count, multiplying by 1-alpha and then adding alpha/N to every entry (lines 300-310).

Source claim: Theorem 21.1 states that an ergodic chain has a unique steady-state vector equal to the principal left eigenvector of P; power iteration is offered as the elementary computation and a three-state example converges to (5/18, 4/9, 5/18) (lines 336-448).

Source claim: topic-specific PageRank teleports only within a topic set S, pages outside the reachable set Y receive zero, and personalized PageRank for a mixed profile is the linear combination 0.6 pi_s + 0.4 pi_p, so a separate vector per user is unnecessary (lines 532-614).

Source claim: HITS assigns hub and authority scores through h <- A a and a <- A^T h, equivalent to power iteration on A A^T and A^T A, and outputs the top-scoring hubs and top-scoring authorities (lines 708-814).

Source claim: the HITS base set adds pages that link to or are linked from the text-matched root set; implementations reportedly suffice with about 200 root pages and about five iterations of Equation 21.8, with additive rather than matrix-vector updates because the graph is sparse (lines 861-906).

Source claim: HITS results for the query 'japan elementary schools' include Japanese and other non-English pages because the query string is ignored once the base set is assembled, an effect the chapter calls emblematic of how HITS functions (lines 885-936).

Source claim: link farms can inflate both PageRank and HITS, PageRank is argued to be more robust to small topology changes partly because of teleportation, and variants including weighted HITS and SALSA are cited (lines 1012-1031).

notes: Source claim: Salton's 1968 definition frames information retrieval as the structure, analysis, organization, storage, searching and retrieval of information; the book treats text as the primary focus while also covering images, video, audio and scanned documents (pp. 1-3).

Source claim: a document differs from a database record because most of its information is relatively unstructured text, so exact matching as in a database or grep gives poor relevance; comparing texts is the core problem (pp. 1-2, 4-5).

Source claim: applications include web, vertical, enterprise, desktop and peer-to-peer search plus advertising, intelligence, science, health care and customer support; tasks include ad hoc search, filtering/tracking, classification and question answering (Table 1.1, pp. 3-4).

Source claim: the three core issues are relevance (topical versus user), evaluation (precision/recall, test collections, TREC, clickthrough logs) and users/information needs (query suggestion, expansion, relevance feedback) (pp. 4-6).

Source claim: retrieval models usually model statistical properties of text, especially word-occurrence counts, rather than linguistic structure; the text traces this stance to Luhn in the 1950s (p. 5).

Source claim: a search engine is the practical application of IR to large-scale text collections; the term originally denoted specialized search hardware and from the mid-1980s named software that compares queries to documents and returns ranked lists (pp. 6-7).

Source claim: configurations differ in constraints — web search crawls terabytes and serves millions of subsecond queries daily, enterprise search spans heterogeneous sources, desktop search must ingest new local documents rapidly (p. 7).

Source claim: search-engine design adds performance (response time, throughput, indexing speed), incorporation of new data (coverage, freshness), scalability, adaptability and application-specific problems such as spam/spamdexing to the IR issues (pp. 8-9; Figure 1.1).

Source claim: 'search engineer' names practitioners who modify, extend, maintain or tune engines; few have IR training, which motivates the book; open-source examples are Lucene, Lemur/Indri and Galago (pp. 7-10).
Inference: the chapter is a framing survey with no original measurements or experiments; references to Autonomy, Vista search and Yahoo date the framing to the late 2000s revision.

notes: Source claim: an architecture consists of software components, their interfaces and their relationships at a chosen abstraction level; UIMA is cited as an integration standard, and the chapter's view is explicitly not code-level (pp. 13-14).

Source claim: the two primary goals are effectiveness (retrieve the most relevant documents) and efficiency (process queries as quickly as possible); specialized indexes and stored text statistics follow from these goals (p. 13).

Source claim: the indexing process is text acquisition, text transformation and index creation, all feeding a document data store; the query process is user interaction, ranking and evaluation, drawing on the index, data store and log data (Figures 2.1-2.2, pp. 14-16).

Source claim: text acquisition covers web, site, focused/topical, enterprise and desktop crawlers; feeds such as RSS/XML; conversion from HTML, XML, PDF and Office formats; and ASCII/Unicode encoding normalization (pp. 17-19).
Source claim: the document data store keeps compressed content plus metadata, links and anchor text, so components can generate summaries without reprocessing original documents (p. 19).

Source claim: text transformation includes a parser/tokenizer (capitalization, hyphenation, apostrophes, Chinese word segmentation), stopping (function words; list-size trade-offs such as 'to be or not to be' and 'down under'), and stemming (fish/fishes/fishing; aggressive versus conservative; Arabic versus Chinese) (pp. 19-22).

Source claim: link extraction supports PageRank-style analysis and anchor text; information extraction adds phrases and named entities; the classifier assigns topical labels, detects spam and non-content, or clusters documents (p. 21-22).

Source claim: index creation gathers document statistics (term counts, positions, collection/group counts, document length), computes weights such as tf.idf with idf = log N/n, inverts term-document information, and distributes indexes by document or term, with replication and peer-to-peer variants (pp. 22-23).

Source claim: user interaction handles query languages (keyword versus Boolean/proximity), query transformation (tokenization, spell checking, suggestion, expansion, relevance feedback) and results output (snippets, highlighting, clustering, advertising, translation) (pp. 23-25).

Source claim: scoring computes a document score as the sum over terms of query weight times document weight, with BM25 and query-likelihood models deferred to Chapter 7; optimization can be term-at-a-time or document-at-a-time, and only safe optimizations preserve exact scores (pp. 25-26).

Source claim: distributed ranking uses a query broker, and caching of indexes or ranked lists reuses popular work; evaluation covers logging (clickthrough, dwell time), ranking analysis with top-weighted measures, and performance analysis often via simulation (pp. 26-28).

Representation note: Figures 2.1 and 2.2 survive only as scattered labels, and component sidebar labels are interleaved with body prose; the score formula is linearized (summation sign on its own line). There are no numbered tables and no missing figures.

notes: Claim (4.2): word frequencies are skewed; Zipf’s law gives r·Pr ≈ 0.1 for English, with AP89 statistics 84,678 documents, 39,749,179 word occurrences, 198,763 vocabulary items and 70,064 singletons (Tables 4.1–4.3).
Claim (4.2.1): Heaps’ law v = k·nβ fits vocabulary growth; typical k is 10–100 and β ≈ 0.5, while the chapter’s AP89 fit is k = 62.95, β = 0.455 and the GOV2 fit is k = 7.34, β = 0.648 (343–413).
Claim (4.2.2): independence-based result-size estimates fabc = (fa·fb·fc)/N² are too low for correlated terms; co-occurrence corrections and C/s sampling estimates are presented as better (482–589).

Claim (4.3.2): tokenization must preserve query/document symmetry; the general strategy parses markup first, then emits lowercase alphanumeric tokens with punctuation as terminators, leaving variants to query transformation (646–754).
Claim (4.3.3): stopping shrinks the index and usually helps effectiveness, but can erase valid all-stopword queries; the chapter recommends indexing stopwords when space permits (756–798).

Claim (4.3.4): stemming is algorithmic or dictionary-based; Porter uses ordered suffix rules, Krovetz checks a dictionary plus exceptions; reported English gains are small, while Arabic gains are cited above 50% (800–1018).

Claim (4.3.5): POS-tagged noun phrases are useful but too slow for large-scale phrase indexing; word n-grams are the cheaper alternative, and Google’s sample reports 1.02 trillion tokens and 13.6 million unigrams (1023–1201).
Claim (4.4–4.5): HTML fields (title, headings, bold, anchor text, URL depth) are ranking features; anchor text is short, externally authored and especially useful for homepage finding (1206–1386).

Claim (4.5.2): PageRank is the stationary probability of a random surfer with random-jump probability λ = 0.15; the chapter gives the iterative algorithm and notes HITS is query-dependent (1411–1630).

Claim (4.5.3–4.6): trackback cycles and comment links motivate rel=nofollow; named-entity extraction is rule-based or HMM-based, with about 90% effectiveness for person/organization/location but little evidence of general search benefit (1632–1911).
Claim (4.7): language-specific tokenization/stemming matters, especially CJK segmentation and bigrams; low-density languages with little online text remain harder (1914–1985).

Inference: the reported corpus sizes and plot values are historical examples from the cited collections, not contemporary measurements; the chapter’s formulas are simplified models. The 2,198 line count treats each form feed as a line terminator; a bare newline count is 2,147.

notes: Claim (5.2): ranking is abstracted as R(Q,D) = Σ_i g_i(Q)f_i(D), pairing document features f_i with query features g_i; most query feature values are zero, so only query-related features need evaluation (lines 127–202).

Claim (5.3.1): intersecting document-ordered lists costs O(max(m,n)) by a merge-style scan, reduced to O(min(m,n)) with list skipping (lines 343–350).

Claim (5.3.4–5.3.6): extents encode fields as position ranges, e.g. author: (1,4), (4,6), (7,9); storing precomputed scores moves work to indexing but loses proximity flexibility; score-ordered lists let a top-k query read only the first k postings (lines 539–630).

Claim (5.4): compression trades space for decode cost; throughput is min(mr,dp) for memory rate m, processor rate p, compression ratio r and decompression factor d, maximized near mr=dp, and the chapter treats only lossless methods (lines 655–714).

Claim (5.4.3–5.4.4): Elias-γ costs 2⌊log2 k⌋+1 bits and Elias-δ about 2log2log2 k+log2 k bits; v-byte stores seven data bits per byte plus a high terminator bit and is the only compression method Galago uses (lines 869–1006; Tables 5.2–5.5).

Claim (5.4.7): for “galago AND animal” (1M vs 300M postings), k=25 minimizes 500,000k+300,000,000/k; binary search raises the optimum to about 208 with 9.2M steps, while the practical optimum is about 100 bytes (lines 1091–1194; Table 5.6 at 1121–1129).

Claim (5.5): a vocabulary/lexicon maps terms to byte offsets; Galago keeps one entry per 32KB of inverted file, so a 32TB index needs under 1GB of vocabulary and each list is found with one disk seek (lines 1225–1250).

readings.revision: Search Engines: Information Retrieval in Practice, free PDF, 2015 update

notes: Claim (6.1, 51-101): short keyword queries averaging two to three words dominate web search; community question-answering queries average about 30 words, but statistical keyword ranking handles long natural-language queries poorly because engines typically rank only documents containing all terms and ignore syntax and semantics.

Claim (6.1, 58-85): legacy intermediary query syntax combines wildcard operators (NEGLECT!) and proximity constraints (/5, /P, quoted phrase), defaulting to Boolean OR when no constraint is given; only quotes and '+' remain common in simple public interfaces.

Claim (6.2.1, 123-162): query processing must mirror document processing to avoid ranking errors, yet stopping and stemming may differ at query time. If documents are unstemmed, query stemming must expand variants (for example fishing to fish) rather than reduce the query to a stem, otherwise unstemmed documents no longer match.

Claim (6.2.1, 163-253): automatically generated stem classes contain errors and can merge police with policy; the Porter 'polic' class has 22 entries. Co-occurrence connected components using Dice, windows W=50-100 and an empirical threshold split such classes, but fish/fishing stayed merged, so query context still decides. N-gram seed classes performed comparably to algorithmic stemming.

Claim (6.2.2, 258-296): about 10-15% of web queries contain spelling errors, and 80% or more of errors are single-character insertions, deletions, substitutions or transpositions under Damerau-Levenshtein distance; run-on word-boundary errors are treated as another single-character class (371-376).

Claim (6.2.2, 377-483): noisy-channel correction ranks candidates by P(e|w)P(w), and a bigram mixture lambda*P(w)+(1-lambda)*P(w|wp) supplies context. Experiments with the cited iterative corrector found the query-log language model most important, word-pair context critical, at least two iterations helpful, and the error model least important; a uniform error model was nearly as effective.

Claim (6.2.3, 566-638): Dice is 2*nab/(na+nb); mutual information is log[P(a,b)/(P(a)P(b))]; expected mutual information weights MI by P(a,b); chi-square compares observed with expected co-occurrence. MI and chi-square favor low-frequency terms, and the restricted chi-square form produces the same term rankings as the full form when N is large (Table 6.2).

Claim (6.2.3, 662-852): TREC tables for 'tropical' and 'fish' show that single-word associations are specialized or generic, that chi-square and MIM favor rare terms, and that even the best lists contain 'virtually nothing' useful for expanding 'tropical fish'; phrase-level Dice yields goldfish, aquarium, coral and similar terms. The authors conclude that single-word association misses query context and recommend query logs and clickthrough, with virtual documents the best collection-only alternative. Inference: these are illustrative historical TREC results, not general rankings.

Claim (6.2.4, 859-984): pseudo-relevance feedback on the raw top 10 pages for 'tropical fish' selects HTML and stopword noise (a 926, td 535, href 495); restricting to snippets and removing stopwords yields tropical 26, fish 28, aquarium 8. Marking the seventh document relevant would increase the weight of 'breeding'. Both are reported effective in the literature but seldom operational: pseudo-relevance feedback is unpredictable when the initial ranking lacks relevant documents, relevance feedback appears mainly in filtering and 'more like this', and alternative-query suggestion is presented as more reliable.

Claim (6.2.5, 1015-1102): results are usually independent of who submitted the query, why or where; profiles built from visited documents are not specific and did not improve average ranking in cited experiments, and raise privacy concerns. Population query-log/clickthrough history and local search are presented as the most useful contextual signals. Local search identifies page regions, detects query locations (10-15% of queries), then ranks with location; more than 35 US places named Springfield illustrate the ambiguity.

Claim (6.3.1, 1150-1283): Luhn's summarizer scores bracketed significant-word spans by the square of significant-word count divided by span length (Figure 6.4 example 4^2/7 = 2.3) and selects top sentences; modern snippet features include heading/first-line position, query-term count, unique terms, longest run and density. Clickthrough-derived guidelines prefer all query terms in the summary, no repetition when terms are in the title, highlighted URLs and readable prose; snippet generation must fetch cached documents and mark sentence boundaries at indexing time.

Claim (6.3.2-6.4, 1298-1376, 1476-1717): sponsored advertisements combine text relevance, advertiser bids and clickthrough popularity, with long-tail queries using general popularity; about 50% of queries in a session are reformulations, and advertisement ranking favors exact query matches, then stemmed matches, then probabilistic expansion. Result clustering must be efficient (snippet-based) and easy to label: monothetic clusters are preferred over polythetic K-means clusters, while manual facets are more understandable but static. Cross-language search translates queries for monolingual engines; dictionary translation is ambiguity-prone, statistical machine translation with parallel corpora is more general, and transliteration produces many name variants (Qaddafi example).

notes: Claim (7.1): a retrieval model is a mathematical framework that formalizes when text is judged relevant and explains a ranking algorithm's assumptions; the chapter separates topical from user relevance and binary from multivalued relevance, and argues probabilistic scores represent uncertainty better than extra relevance levels (41-78).

Claim (7.1.1): Boolean/exact-match retrieval treats every retrieved document as equally relevant. Its advantages are predictable results, operands beyond words (dates, document type) and scoring efficiency; its drawback is that effectiveness depends entirely on user query formulation, and NOT tends to remove relevant documents (87-180).

Claim (7.1.2): the vector space model represents documents and queries as t-dimensional term-weight vectors and ranks by cosine similarity; the chapter states there is no theoretical reason to prefer cosine, only empirical performance, and gives tf.idf weights with log tf and log(N/nk). Rocchio query modification uses alpha, beta, gamma of 8, 16, 4 and typically adds about 50 high-weight terms from relevant documents (196-426).

Claim (7.2-7.2.1): the Probability Ranking Principle ranks documents by decreasing probability of relevance and is optimal under independence assumptions, but does not itself specify how to estimate relevance (440-465). The binary independence model applies a Bayes decision rule with term independence (acknowledged as false for natural text) and binary features; with pi = 0.5 and si approximated by ni/N the weight reduces to log((N-ni)/ni), an idf-like weight with no tf component (522-652).

Claim (7.2.2): BM25 adds document and query term frequencies plus length normalization to the binary independence model, with typical k1 = 1.2, b = 0.75 and k2 in 0-1,000. In the worked example (N = 500,000; n1 = 40,000; n2 = 300; f1 = 15; f2 = 25; dl/avdl = 0.9) K = 1.11 and the score is 20.66; Table 7.2 shows 15.66 for 0/25 versus 12.74 for 15/1. The authors call BM25 experimentally strong and commercially influential but 'not a formal model' (713-824).

Claim (7.3.1): query likelihood ranks by P(Q|D) using a unigram document model; maximum-likelihood estimates give zero for missing query words, so Jelinek-Mercer smoothing mixes document and collection probabilities with lambda about 0.1 for short and 0.7 for long queries, while Dirichlet smoothing uses mu typically 1,000-2,000 and is described as generally more effective. The worked query-likelihood score is -10.53, and the authors report effectiveness comparable to BM25 and better on most TREC collections (935-1197).

Claim (7.3.2): the relevance model treats the query as a small sample from a relevance model estimated from top-ranked documents; ranking compares that model with document models by negative KL divergence in two passes, typically using 10-50 top documents and 10-25 expansion words with lambda = 0.5 mixing. The authors call it one of the best pseudo-relevance feedback methods but note improvements are inconsistent; Tables 7.4-7.5 list 16 high-probability terms for four queries using top 10 versus top 50 documents (1207-1462).

Claim (7.4.1-7.4.2): the inference network is a directed acyclic graph of binary events; representation nodes use language-model probabilities with Dirichlet smoothing, a multiple-Bernoulli multiset captures term frequency, and query nodes implement NOT, OR, AND, weighted AND, max, sum and weighted sum. #combine and #weight are geometric-mean normalizations, and weighted AND over single terms reproduces query-likelihood ranking (1509-1719). The Galago language adds #od/#uw proximity, #syn/#wsyn, contexts and extents, #filter, and #prior (1721-1947).

Claim (7.5): web search differs by collection size, links, document types, query volume and query intent; the chapter uses Broder's informational/navigational/transactional taxonomy and groups ranking evidence into page content, metadata, anchor text, links and user behavior. It reports that only about 50% of TREC-judged relevant topical pages contain all query terms, so Boolean-AND filtering is risky, and that the dependence model uses exact phrases plus #uw:8/#uw:12 windows. In TREC .gov experiments body text was most important, and query expansion helped topical but hurt navigational searches (1952-2129).

Claim (7.6.1-7.6.2): generative models estimate a document distribution, while discriminative models such as Ranking SVM learn pairwise rank preferences from judgments or clickthrough, with slack variables and C controlling overfitting; learned linear weights can be used directly in inference-network queries. Topic models address vocabulary mismatch: LSI/LSA reduces dimensionality, and LDA models each document as a mixture of about 400 topics whose probabilities can smooth query likelihood, but estimation is expensive and limited to smaller collections (2165-2429).

Claim (7.7): application guidance is to build a queries/documents/judgments test collection, select content, proximity, structure and numeric features, use an application thesaurus through a #syn-like operator rather than adding words, and tune parameters using published values as a starting point. The chapter names BM25, query likelihood, relevance models, inference networks and Ranking SVM as its ranking blueprints (2433-2485). Inference: these are textbook syntheses of cited TREC experiments; I did not reproduce any experiment, and the chapter's improvement percentages and parameter recommendations are reported claims, not verified measurements.

sections.heading: Training, Testing, and Statistics; Significance Tests

notes: Claim (8.1): effectiveness measures how well a ranking matches relevance judgments, efficiency measures time and space, and cost is the third constraint; the authors state that no reliable technique that significantly improves effectiveness is currently excluded for efficiency reasons, and distinguish parameter optimization from search-engine optimization (9-93). Inference: the chapter treats controlled batch experiments as the primary evidence standard and leaves holistic interactive evaluation aside.

Claim (8.2): Cranfield-style test collections fix documents, queries and judgments. Table 8.1 gives CACM 3,204 documents/2.2 MB/64 words, AP 242,918/0.7 GB/474 and GOV2 25,205,179/426 GB/1,073; Table 8.2 gives 64, 100 and 150 queries with 16, 220 and 180 relevant documents per query (96-198).

Claim (8.2): pooling merges the top k = 50-200 results per system and can treat unpooled relevant documents as non-relevant, which the chapter says would penalize a new algorithm; TREC studies are said to show judgments complete enough for comparisons. The query-count analysis says 25 queries give a wrong conclusion about a 0.05 MAP difference in about 13% of comparisons, 50 queries below 4%, and a 10% relative MAP difference suffices with a significance test (245-305).

Claim (8.3): logs record a user or session identifier, the exact query, ranked URLs with click flags and timestamps; dwell time and exit action are among the best implicit predictors. Clicks are biased toward high ranks and popular pages, so Skip Above and Skip Next converts clicks into preferences, and the click deviation CD(d,p)=O(d,p)-E(p) filters unusually frequent clicks (338-440).

Claim (8.4.1): recall is |A intersect B|/|A| and precision is |A intersect B|/|B|; fallout covers false positives but is vanishingly small on skewed collections, so precision is preferred as user-facing. F is the harmonic mean and F-beta reweights recall against precision. Average precision for the worked rankings is 0.78 versus 0.52 (452-664).

Claim (8.4.2): MAP averages per-query average precision (worked 0.62 and 0.44 for two queries, MAP 0.53); interpolation P(R)=max{P':R'>=R} produces a step function, and Table 8.4 averages precision at the 11 standard recall levels. Macro-averaging versus micro-averaging is explained in a footnote (666-843).

Claim (8.4.3): for top-heavy tasks the chapter presents precision at p (usually 10 or 20), MRR (worked reciprocal ranks 0.5 and 0.2, MRR 0.35) and DCG/NDCG with a log2 discount (worked DCG 6.89 at rank 5 and 9.61 at rank 10; NDCG values up to 0.88). It states there is no theoretical justification for this discount and gives an alternative exponential-gain definition used by some companies (900-1010).

Claim (8.4.4): Kendall tau = (P-Q)/(P+Q) compares full preference rankings (worked 0.33 when 10 of 15 preferences agree), but the authors say no studies are available showing tau is useful for comparing systems. BPREF balances R relevant documents against the first R non-relevant ones, ranges 0-1, and is reported as robust and similar to MAP for system comparisons (1012-1066).

Claim (8.5): efficiency metrics include elapsed and CPU indexing time, query throughput, latency, indexing temporary space and index size (Table 8.5). Throughput and latency trade off, latency is often reported as a percentile bound, and operations under about 150 ms are described as perceived instantaneous (1068-1165).

Claim (8.6.1): significance testing uses a null hypothesis, one-tailed tests, Type I/II errors and power. On the artificial 10-query data in Table 8.6 the paired t-test gives a mean difference of 21.4, standard deviation 29.1, t=2.33 and p=0.02; Wilcoxon gives w=35 and p about 0.025; the sign test finds 7 of 10 and p=0.17, so it cannot reject. A 5% average-precision difference (10% conservative) is cited as the old noticeable-difference threshold (1167-1382).

Claim (8.6.2-8.6.3): parameters must be tuned on training data and compared once on test data, with cross-validation as the fallback; testing on training data is the 'cardinal sin' and brute-force parameter sweeps are exhaustive but expensive. Online testing uses live traffic, often 1-5%, and provides cheap but noisy click data while risking the user experience (1384-1507).

Claim (8.7): no single effectiveness measure is correct; the recommended bundle is MAP, average NDCG, a recall-precision graph and precision at 10, always against a baseline, with the t-test and a per-query improvement distribution (Fig. 8.9); Galago provides the measures. Inference: the evidence base is TREC-centric, and interactive evaluation is only pointed to via Belkin (2008) (1510-1654).

notes: Claim (intro): classification is supervised labeling and clustering is unsupervised grouping; the chapter positions both as machine-learning tasks that are heavily used in search engines and explicitly limits itself to an overview rather than theory (8-65).

Claim (9.1): ontology choice (binary, multivalued or hierarchical) must fit the task and the available labels; collapsing rare labels into a coarser class can improve generalization. A human-classification analogy leads to feature extraction, a weighted evidence score H(food)=sum w_i f_i, and a threshold decision rule (68-137).

Claim (9.1.1): Naive Bayes applies Bayes' rule with class priors P(c)=Nc/N and a conditional-independence factorization P(d|c)=product P(wi|c); the multiple-Bernoulli and multinomial event spaces are contrasted with worked spam tables and estimates such as P(the|spam)=4/20 and P(dinner|not spam)=1/15 (139-453).

Claim (9.1.1): maximum likelihood gives zero probabilities for unseen term-class pairs, so the chapter presents Bayesian smoothing (df+alpha)/(N+alpha+beta), add-one, and a Dirichlet-style estimate with mu; it states the multinomial model consistently outperforms multiple-Bernoulli and that training reduces to term statistics that usually fit in memory (352-516).

Claim (9.1.2): SVMs find the maximum-margin separating hyperplane; with w.x-=-1 and w.x+=1 the margin is 2/||w||, leading to minimizing 0.5||w||^2 subject to per-class constraints. Non-separable data adds hinge loss and slack variables with penalty C (standard C=1), solved by quadratic programming (518-721).

Claim (9.1.2): the kernel trick computes dot products in an implicit higher-dimensional space; the worked mapping Phi(x)=[x1^2, sqrt(2)x1x2, x2^2] gives Phi(w).Phi(x)=(w.x)^2, and Table 9.1 lists linear, polynomial and Gaussian (RBF, infinite-dimensional) kernels. Multi-class classification uses one-versus-all or one-versus-one, with no stated preference between them (723-847).

Claim (9.1.3-9.1.4): classification reuses accuracy, precision, recall, F and ROC from Chapter 8, but micro-averaging is widely used in classification where retrieval rarely uses it. Generative models (Naive Bayes) can win with few examples, discriminative models (SVMs) often win as data grows, and non-parametric nearest-neighbor can fit nonlinear boundaries but has high variance on small samples. Information gain IG(w)=H(C)-H(C|w) selects features; the worked IG(cheap)=0.2749 and IG(dinner)=0.3612 make 'dinner' the best predictor and 'the' useless (849-1050).

Claim (9.1.5): spam is defined subjectively and split into link spam (blog links, exchanges, farms) and term spam (repetition, dumping, phrase stitching, weaving); SpamAssassin combines a Bayes score with blacklists and date checks. Ntoulas et al. report above 90% accuracy from content features such as compressibility and n-gram likelihood (1054-1245).

Claim (9.1.5): sentiment pipelines need opinion detection, information extraction and polarity classification; Pang et al. report an SVM on unigrams above 80% versus about 60% for a human word-list baseline, and multiple-Bernoulli beat multinomial there. For ads, Broder et al. classify into a manually built hierarchy of over 6,000 nodes using tf.idf cosine and score semantic distance by least-common-ancestor depth (1265-1444).

Claim (9.2-9.2.1): clustering is ill-defined and usually polythetic; a similarity S converts to distance 1-S. Hierarchical clustering is divisive or agglomerative; Algorithm 1 merges the cheapest pair until K clusters, with single, complete, average, average-group and Ward cost functions. The chapter reports average-link generally best in IR experiments, O(N^2) cost, and that no single algorithm is best (1447-1813).

Claim (9.2.1-9.2.2): K-means keeps K fixed and minimizes sum dist(Xi,Ck), typically squared Euclidean (cosine in spherical K-means); it is heuristic, initialization- and order-dependent, but O(KN). K-nearest-neighbor clustering creates one overlapping cluster per instance, is O(N^2), and is used for language-model smoothing, score smoothing and pseudo-relevance feedback (1817-1977).

Claim (9.2.3-9.2.5): cluster evaluation uses ClusterPrecision = sum |MaxClass(Ci)|/N when labels exist, otherwise an objective function, which the authors call circular; choosing K has no formula, and Parzen windows replace K with a window size. The cluster hypothesis ('closely associated documents tend to be relevant to the same requests') is tested by similarity distributions and local precision, with Fig. 9.18 showing poor separation but high local precision on trec12. Cluster-based retrieval gives small, variable gains; cluster smoothing gives 'significant and consistent' gains, yet cost has kept both out of operational ranking, with query-specific clustering as the recent exception (1979-2261).

notes: Claim (10.1): social search is defined very broadly as search within an environment where a community of users actively participates — defining profiles and interests, interacting with other users, and modifying representations of the objects searched — in contrast to standard models that treat every user the same and restrict interaction to query formulation (9-48); the chapter scopes five topics — user tags, communities, filtering and recommender systems, P2P search and metasearch — and explicitly defers personalization to section 6.2.5, because it supplies query context rather than a social setting (9-120).

Claim (10.2): social tagging is manual indexing by end users with little quality control and no fixed vocabulary, so tag sets form folksonomies described as dynamic, community-influenced ontologies; this differs from expert card catalogs built from a controlled vocabulary, and the chapter reports evaluations in which automatic indexing is at least as effective and manual plus automatic is most effective (123-208).

Claim (10.2.1): tags are sparse representations of complex items, so conjunctive queries favour precision and disjunctive queries recall; vocabulary mismatch is reduced by pseudo-relevance-feedback-style enrichment of tags or queries from web search snippets (Figure 10.1), and tags are additionally noisy and often missing (213-304).

Claim (10.2.2): missing tags can be inferred by tf.idf term selection, by one binary classifier per tag trained on existing tag/item pairs (an SVM over page text, anchor text and link features), or by Maximal Marginal Relevance, which trades relevance against redundancy through lambda (306-376).

Claim (10.2.3): tag-chain browsing is focused but offers no global view, so popular tags and tag clouds (weighted lists whose display size tracks popularity or importance) are used to start exploration (378-451).

Claim (10.3.2): community finding operates on directed or undirected graphs with two criteria — member similarity and denser interaction inside than outside — and the chapter presents HITS (iterative authority/hub scores with normalization, Algorithm 3, Figures 10.3-10.4) and clustering over node vectors; it states that community-finding effectiveness cannot be compared cleanly because community membership is ill-defined (502-759).

Claim (10.3.3): community-based question answering is preferred for needs no single page satisfies, and archived questions are better match targets than archived answers; vocabulary mismatch is addressed with intralanguage translation models — Berger and Lafferty's translated query likelihood and Xue et al.'s interpolation with beta and Dirichlet smoothing — with translation probabilities estimated from question/answer pairs treated as a parallel corpus and truncated to the top few translations per term for cost (761-961).

Claim (10.3.4): collaborative search splits into co-located (CoSearch: driver, observers, shared page queue and query queue) and remote (SearchTogether: persistent sessions, shared and refinable query logs, ratings, comments, recommendations), and the chapter notes that very few commercial systems exist (963-1064).

Claim (10.4.1): filtering fixes a long-term profile while documents stream in, so it is a push application and a supervised task with very little training data; static models reuse retrieval models plus a score threshold (a language-model profile ranked by negative KL divergence is given in full), adaptive models update profiles through Rocchio, relevance models or online learning, millions of profiles are matched by indexing profiles and treating each incoming document as a query, and evaluation uses set-based measures from a contingency table including U = alpha*TP + beta*TN + delta*FP + gamma*FN (1068-1470).

Claim (10.4.2): collaborative filtering exploits relationships between profiles, associates one profile per user, predicts ratings rather than binary retrieval decisions and revisits all previously unjudged items; the chapter gives user clustering with correlation similarity, average and expected-rating prediction, nearest-neighbour prediction with user-mean offsets (more robust and empirically stronger than clustering), and evaluation by absolute error and mean squared error rather than strict accuracy (1472-1752).

Claim (10.5): distributed search requires resource representation, resource selection and result merging; nodes are described by a unigram language model (or by query-based sampling when they expose only a search API), ranked by query likelihood, and merged by local scores when models and statistics agree, otherwise by normalized scores or CombMNZ; reported TREC evidence is that selecting 5-10 of 200 collections matched centralized search while selecting 1% of 2,500 P2P nodes cost 25% average precision at rank 10, and four-engine metasearch gained 5-20% MAP over the best single engine; the P2P architectures are central hub, pure flooding with a hop horizon, and hierarchical superpeers, plus DHT/Chord exact-match routing in O(log N) hops (1754-2074).

Inference (not a source claim): the chapter's own framing makes its filtering and recommender material the closest analogue to operational profile stores and recommendation surfaces, while its distributed-search material is the closest analogue to result merging across heterogeneous backends; the text supplies no architecture, latency, failure or cost evidence for either, because Figure 10.11's topologies and all quantitative settings are extracted only as captions and label fragments.

readings.coverage: Chapter 11 complete: PDF pp. 451-485, sections 11.1-11.7 (including 11.4.1-11.4.2), Tables 11.1-11.2, figure captions 11.1-11.12, the three Galago query listings (independence, sequential and full dependence), References and Further Reading, and Exercises 11.1-11.13; 1,376 splitlines and 12,187 words. All body prose read sequentially; running heads, page numbers, form-feed page breaks and layout whitespace excluded from analysis. Figure raster/diagram content is absent from the text extraction (see representation_gap).
readings.omissions: Other book chapters outside this batch not read; no reproduction or experiment
readings.representation_gap: Figures 11.1-11.12 are images. Only detached labels survive: 11.1 leaves D, q1, q2, q3 four times but no edges, so the independence/sequential/full/general panels are indistinguishable; 11.2 leaves the two D nodes and the query words plus two question marks; 11.3 turns capability markers into '!' bullets; 11.5 leaves the QA pipeline labels scattered across lines; 11.8 leaves only the caption (the two images and their hue histograms are absent); 11.9 leaves only the caption (the car/train/trademark examples are absent); 11.10 leaves only the caption; 11.11 keeps the five annotation word lists but not the images; 11.12 leaves only the caption. Figure 11.6's two 'Original' panels are blank while their OCR outputs survive as noisy text, and Figure 11.7's transcript and recognizer output survive as text. Equations are layout-degraded: the scoring sum in 11.2 is displaced above its body (70-72), the parameter hat and arg max split across lines (97-98), the entity-ranking summation and the P(q|e,d) normalizer Z are split (574-576, 595-603), and the Gaussian kernel prints flattened as 'exp −||q − e||2 /2σ 2' (617). The Galago #weight listings lose closing parentheses at 232-236 and 268-275, so operator nesting must be reconstructed from the surrounding prose. Table 11.2's two-column alignment is fragile where question text wraps. Ligatures (ff, fi, fl) and other typographic artifacts are present, and footnotes are interleaved at page breaks. Running heads ('452 11 Beyond Bag of Words' etc.) and page numbers occur on every page and were excluded from reading and from the reported word count.
notes: Claim (11.1): bag of words denotes a document as an unordered collection of words with no syntactic or statistical relations; query likelihood, BM25 and the vector space model all rest on it, and although linguistically poor it has been hard to beat — even phrase and proximity features took years to yield consistent gains (9-34); the chapter then selects four representation aspects to examine — term dependencies, document structure, query structure for question answering and non-text features — before speculating about the future of search (9-59).

Claim (11.2): linear feature-based models restrict the scoring function to S_Lambda(D;Q) = sum_j lambda_j * f_j(D,Q) + Z, learn Lambda by maximizing an evaluation metric over training data, use brute-force search for few features and the Ranking SVM otherwise, and are preferred because features are easy to add and optimization is efficient; the standard topical feature set is term occurrence, term frequency, idf, document length and proximity (61-131).

Claim (11.3): the Markov Random Field model is an undirected graphical model with a document node connected to every query term node; four dependency assumptions are distinguished (full independence, sequential, full, general), potential functions over cliques may compute exact-phrase or window counts, and the text reports that sequential dependence is the best practical choice because attempts to learn dependencies have come up short (133-222).

Claim (11.3): Galago expresses the model directly — #combine for independence, and #weight(0.8 #combine(terms) 0.1 #combine(#od:1 adjacent pairs) 0.1 #combine(#uw:8 adjacent pairs)) for sequential dependence, with the full-dependence variant adding #od:1 triples, #uw:8 non-adjacent pairs and #uw:12 triples; the 0.8/0.1/0.1 weights are described as empirically derived and show individual terms dominate (223-283).

Claim (11.3): latent concept expansion extends pseudo-relevance feedback inside the MRF by modelling dependencies among expansion words, so multiword concepts can be proposed instead of single words; Table 11.1 lists the top one- and two-word concepts for 'hubble telescope achievements' on TREC ROBUST (284-341).

Claim (11.4): compared with a relational database the search engine offers no schema, no attribute data types and no joins; documents are contexts defined by tag pairs and stored with primary-key access only, while the database contributes persistence, reliability, scalability and a simple API, with BigTable cited as a precedent for dropping schema and joins (342-436).

Claim (11.4.1): XML retrieval is evaluated through INEX content-and-structure queries written in NEXI, whose paths and path filters combine element structure with textual predicates; the chapter reports that people rarely use structural cues, often use them incorrectly, and that there is essentially no evidence structure in user queries improves effectiveness, so INEX moved toward content-only queries and automatic element ranking (438-519).

Claim (11.4.2): entity search ranks entities rather than documents by building pseudo-documents from words near each mention, then estimating P(e,q) = sum_d P(e,q|d)P(d) decomposed as P(q|e,d)P(e|d); independence between words and entities loses effectiveness, so co-occurrence proximity with a Gaussian kernel is used, and accurate named-entity recognition was found not to matter much for expert search (523-624).

Claim (11.5): question answering pipelines combine question analysis/classification into about 31 answer-type categories, passage retrieval and answer selection; useful features include expected entity type, question words, answer patterns and thesaurus relations, and the text states that benefits for non-factoid questions have yet to be shown in retrieval experiments (626-795).

Claim (11.6): OCR and speech recognition inject character-level and OOV errors but TREC-style evaluations show little effectiveness loss because collections are redundant, except for short documents and high error rates; image retrieval uses quantized colour histograms, texture and shape plus key frames for video and relevance-model annotation over image terms, and music retrieval uses spectral-peak signatures and query-by-humming with adapted n-gram and language models (797-1108).

Claim (11.7): the closing argument predicts continued proliferation of specialized search services alongside convergence on probabilistic and linear feature-based models, closer coupling of implementation choice to efficiency and adaptability, and future interfaces that model users, tasks and dialog far more explicitly than current engines do (1110-1196).

Inference (not a source claim): the chapter's strongest operational content is the feature-weight and operator-nesting structure of the Galago listings, whereas its evidence for structure, entity, question and multimedia retrieval is narrative and citation-based; the extracted text preserves no measurements from Figures 11.8-11.12, so image and music claims cannot be checked against the figures themselves.

readings.unit: R230 / Asterisk chapter
readings.revision: The Architecture of Open Source Applications, Volume I, public HTML
readings.coverage: Full: 100% of assigned file (376/376 lines, 5128/5128 words); introduction, Sections 1.1-1.5, code examples and footnotes.
readings.omissions: Other AOSA chapters outside this batch not read; no production experiment. Figure images not transcribed; no Asterisk source tree or external documentation inspected; live-site navigation/footer excluded.
readings.representation_gap: Live page contains 8 figures (PNG); the local representation retains their captions but not image content, so diagram-only information is unavailable. All 16 numbered section headings plus Footnotes match the live page. Superscript footnote markers are flattened into adjacent words (e.g. 'Asterisk1', 'DTMF key2'); code blocks are delimited by extractor tags [CODE]/[/CODE].
notes: Source: Asterisk is a GPLv2 open-source telephony platform for making, receiving and custom-processing calls; Mark Spencer started it in 1999 at Linux Support Services, later Digium.
Source: a channel represents one connection between Asterisk and an endpoint and is an ast_channel; a bridge passes media between channels, with all media negotiated through Asterisk.

Source: bridging is either generic (technology-agnostic, flexible, least efficient due to abstraction) or native (technology-specific, selected by comparing C function pointers when both channels support the same method).

Source: communication inside a call uses ast_frame media or signalling frames; frame types are statically defined (VOICE, VIDEO, MODEM, CONTROL, DTMF_BEGIN, DTMF_END), and MODEM data must remain undisturbed whereas audio may be transcoded.

Source: the core in main/ acts mainly as a module registry; loadable modules register implementations of component abstractions at runtime, and configuration can restrict and order module loading for memory and security benefits.

Source: the channel driver interface ast_channel_tech defines requester, call, answer, hangup, indicate, send_digit_begin/end, read, write and bridge; technology-specific operations are deferred to the driver.

Source: the dialplan in extensions.conf is a set of extensions selecting applications from a runtime-populated registry (~200 applications); dialplan functions mostly set or retrieve channel metadata and do not signal or process media; codec translators implement ast_translator with source and destination formats.

Source: Asterisk is heavily multithreaded over POSIX threads; network monitor threads handle connection setup per channel driver, then one channel thread per inbound channel executes the dialplan and owns ast_channel lifetime.

Source: voicemail and bridged-call walkthroughs show component interaction; Dial allocates an outbound channel, the inbound call is not answered until the outbound is answered, and both channels receive technology-specific hangup handling.

Source limitation claims: cross-server scaling is not well addressed, with Asterisk SCF named as a companion project; complex audio and video codec negotiation is described as weak and a top development priority.
Extractor artifacts: figures 1.1-1.8 are captions only locally; footnote markers are flattened; code examples are preserved but wrapped in [CODE] tags.
Inference (reader): the chapter reports design rationale and practitioner experience, not benchmarks or measured efficiency results; no performance experiment is present.

readings.unit: R231 / Audacity chapter
readings.revision: The Architecture of Open Source Applications, Volume I, public HTML
readings.coverage: Full: 100% of assigned file (286/286 lines, 6303/6303 words); introduction, Sections 2.1-2.9 and footnote.
readings.omissions: Other AOSA chapters outside this batch not read; no production experiment. Figure images and screenshots not inspected; no Audacity source tree, build, or external documentation inspected; live-site navigation/footer excluded.
readings.representation_gap: Live page contains 6 figures (PNG); the local representation retains their captions but not image content, so diagram and screenshot information is unavailable. All 9 numbered section headings plus Footnotes match the live page. The single footnote superscript is flattened into adjacent text ('could want.1'); the code sample is wrapped in extractor tags [CODE]/[/CODE].
notes: Source: Audacity is a popular sound recorder and audio editor; Dominic Mazzoni wrote the original in 1999 as a Carnegie Mellon research student, and the same source compiles for Windows, Linux and Mac.
Source: user-interface discoverability is an explicit goal, but there is no overall architecture; the author uses a 'small city' analogy with impressive buildings and run-down neighborhoods.
Source: Audacity layers on PortAudio and wxWidgets, with optional LADSPA, VAMP, libFLAC, libogg and libvorbis; MP3 support dynamically loads LAME or FFmpeg and VST is excluded because of licensing.
Source: FFTW is offered only in self-compiled builds because the authors argue its license conflicts with Audacity's plugin support; the chapter presents this as a trade-off, not a legal ruling.
Source: a rule against any TCP/IP connection to or from Audacity reduces security exposure, reflecting the small team's limited resources.

Source: ShuttleGui is a facade between wxWidgets and Audacity that shortens dialog code and shuttles data both ways between GUI and preferences; dialogs are compiled into code, and the custom toolbar predates wxWidgets' toolbar.

Source: TrackPanel is a custom-drawn control mixing GUI and application code; a flyweight/sizer redesign was attempted but blocked by flicker risk, wxWidgets slowdown with many widgets, and disagreement about the target design.

Source: BlockFiles are roughly 1 MB chunks coordinated by an XML .aup master file, reference-counted to support undo until save, never internally sparse, and accompanied by summary BlockFiles for zoomed-out drawing; imported .wav spans are no longer the default because users lost originals, and Windows performance led to subdirectories of at most 100 files.

Source: three thread roles handle audio - a PortAudio pthread callback filling five-second buffers, an AudioIO thread moving data to tracks/disk through FillBuffers, and the wxWidgets GUI thread updating on a 20 Hz timer; shared variables replace mutexes by design.

Source: scripting is an experimental optional DLL exposing textual commands over a named pipe, with a security warning; the CleanSpeech fork-avoidance work produced batch chains and preceded scripting.

Source: Audacity has no real-time effects; on-demand loading (background summary generation, out-of-order block processing) is described as an evolutionary step, with block overlap and varying parameters still needed for real-time effects.
Extractor artifacts: figures 2.1-2.6 are captions only locally; the footnote marker is flattened; no section is missing. No benchmarks or production experiment appear in the chapter.

readings.unit: R232 / The Bourne-Again Shell (AOSA Volume I, chapter 3)
readings.revision: The Architecture of Open Source Applications, Volume I, public HTML
readings.coverage: Full chapter read end-to-end: 452/452 lines and 7,489/7,489 whitespace-delimited words, SHA-256 matched to manifest R232. All numbered sections 3.1-3.8, their subsections and both footnotes accounted for. Analysis excluded the L8 site banner and 292 whitespace-only spacer lines; the reported counts cover the whole local file including chrome and [CODE] markers.
readings.omissions: Other AOSA chapters outside this batch not read; no production experiment
sections: 3.7.1. What I Have Found Is Important (L400)
3.7.2. What I Would Have Done Differently (L424)
notes: Source claim: the chapter organizes bash as a staged pipeline — terminal/file input, readline or buffered input, lexical analysis and yacc/bison parsing, word expansion, then command execution — and uses that pipeline as its architectural lens (L20-L23, L316-L319).

Source claim: the implementation rests on a small set of structures (arrays, trees, singly and doubly linked lists, hash tables); WORD_DESC and WORD_LIST carry words between stages, with flags carrying stage state such as assignment markers or a quoted null string (L92-L121, L310).

Source claim: interactive editing is delegated to readline, a read/dispatch/execute/redisplay loop whose keymaps are dispatch tables; applications extend it through bindable functions and hook-function pointers, and bash adds more than thirty bindable commands (L136-L169).

Source claim: non-interactive input must respect POSIX consumption rules — buffer only when the file offset can be rolled back to the parser's stopping point, and read character by character from non-seekable input (L175-L178).

Source claim: the parser is context-dependent, saves and restores parser state around recursive command-substitution and completion parsing, and rewinds read-ahead input; the author calls it the only Bourne-style shell parser built with Yacc or Bison (L193-L227).

Source claim: word expansion is itself a pipeline (brace, tilde, parameter, command and process substitution, arithmetic, IFS splitting, globbing); quote style determines which expansions apply (L245-L307).

Source claim: redirection needs an undo list with distinct lifetimes for shell functions, the '.' builtin and 'exec'; allowing descriptors above 9 forces bookkeeping of internal descriptors and close-on-exec heuristics (L331-L343).

Source claim: job control represents a job as a process list plus state and process-group ID; the terminal's foreground process group decides which job may read, and synchronizing child creation with process-group assignment is the hard part (L379-L385).

Source claim: the author's lessons are detailed change logs, regression tests, standards participation, internal standards, authoritative documentation, reuse and community engagement; he would add formal compatibility levels, more frequent releases using a public repository and a hand-written recursive-descent parser (L403-L433).

Inference: the pipeline description is a conceptual decomposition, not a strictly one-way runtime sequence — command substitution, programmable completion and prompt expansion re-enter the parser during later stages (L221-L227).
Inference: scale statements such as 'millions of users' and the Yacc/Bison uniqueness claim are author assertions; this read found no measurement or independent corroboration in the chapter.

readings.unit: R233 / Berkeley DB (AOSA Volume I, chapter 4)
readings.revision: The Architecture of Open Source Applications, Volume I, public HTML
readings.coverage: Full chapter read end-to-end: 441/441 lines and 9,571/9,571 whitespace-delimited words, SHA-256 matched to manifest R233. All numbered sections 4.1-4.10, their subsections, fourteen inline 'Design Lesson' passages, Tables 4.1-4.2 and the footnote accounted for. Analysis excluded the L8 site banner and 284 whitespace-only spacer lines; counts cover the whole local file including chrome and flattening artifacts.
readings.omissions: Other AOSA chapters outside this batch not read; no production experiment
sections: 4.3. The Access Methods: Btree, Hash, Recno, Queue (L104)
notes: Source claim: Berkeley DB began as a freely redistributable replacement for in-memory hsearch and on-disk dbm/ndbm; Seltzer's hash used Litwin extensible linear hashing, Olson added a Btree, and the two were unified behind access-method-agnostic database handles before the LIBTP paper and the 4BSD 1.85 release (L23-L35).

Source claim: the timeline is 1996 Netscape contract, 2.0 in 1997 adding transactions, 3.0 in 1999 adding abstraction, 4.0 in 2001 adding replication and Oracle 5.0 in 2010 adding SQL; the authors present this as incremental adaptation of a modular design (L38-L44).

Source claim: the architecture is a cooperating set of modules — access methods, interface layer, Mpool, lock, log/dbreg and transaction — now sharing a DB_ENV handle; components remain independently usable and all functions return error codes up the call stack (L98-L188).

Source claim: four snapshots trace evolution — LIBTP without a process manager, the intended 2.0 design, actual 2.0.6 adding general recovery, and 5.0.21 adding replication, splitting log/dbreg, a cursor-based log API and a fileop module (L59-L83).

Source claim: public calls pass through _pp interface wrappers, _arg checks and a worker; the interface layer tracks threads inside the library, generates implicit transactions and performs generic plus per-call validation (L140-L167).

Source claim: Mpool caches file pages and represents inter-page pointers as page numbers because the on-disk format is also the in-memory format; every access pins a page, and distinguishing read from write pins enabled multi-version concurrency control (L200-L212).

Source claim: write-ahead logging is enforced by an LSN stored on each page; set_lsn_offset and set_clearlen let Mpool enforce WAL without requiring every Mpool client to adopt Berkeley DB's page format (L218-L227).

Source claim: the lock manager uses 32-bit locker IDs split between transactions and non-transactions, opaque lock objects, a square conflict matrix, intention locks, atomic multi-lock lock_vec and lock coupling; page-level locking was chosen for recovery stability over concurrency (L236-L293).

Source claim: the log is a set of sequentially numbered append-only files; LSNs are file-number/offset pairs, headers carry length, previous-record offset and checksum, log_flush supports WAL, and checkpoint records are a deliberate abstraction violation cached for performance (L308-L347).
Source claim: dbreg was pulled out of the log subsystem after repeated bug fixes, and the authors say the filename-to-log-file-id mapping should logically have lived with the environment (L350-L353).

Source claim: recovery is a five-step scheme — find the checkpoint before the checkpoint LSN, read forward to rebuild dbreg mappings and the committed list, read backward undoing uncommitted transactions, read forward redoing committed ones, then checkpoint (L392-L424).

Inference: the fourteen 'Design Lesson' passages are experience-based generalizations, not controlled findings; the chapter reports no benchmark, incident count or comparative experiment, and 'most widely used database toolkit' with hundreds of millions of deployments (L44) is an author claim not verified here.

readings.unit: R234 / CMake (AOSA Volume I, chapter 5)
readings.revision: The Architecture of Open Source Applications, Volume I, public HTML
readings.coverage: Full chapter read end-to-end: 269/269 lines and 4,045/4,045 whitespace-delimited words, SHA-256 matched to manifest R234. All numbered sections 5.1-5.3, their subsections and the footnote accounted for. Analysis excluded the L8 site banner and 159 whitespace-only spacer lines; counts cover the whole local file, including four C-preprocessor lines mis-rendered as Markdown H1 headings.
readings.omissions: Other AOSA chapters outside this batch not read; no production experiment
notes: Source claim: in 1999 the National Library of Medicine engaged Kitware to improve configuration, build and deployment for ITK; CMake emerged as a replacement for the autoconf/libtool approach and grew into CMake, CTest, CPack and CDash (L11-L14).

Source claim: the stated constraints were a C++ compiler as the only dependency, Visual Studio project generation, easy static/shared/executable/plugin targets, build-time code generators, out-of-source builds, system introspection, automatic C/C++ header dependency scanning and consistent behavior on every supported platform (L32-L48).

Source claim: avoiding extra dependencies forced CMake to define its own simple language; the authors acknowledge this limits features to what IDEs support and remains an adoption objection, while arguing Tcl would have been harder to build and less popular (L51-L57).

Source claim: operation has two phases — configure parses CMakeCache.txt and CMakeLists.txt, executes each command through a C++ command object, and builds an in-memory tree of cmMakefile objects holding cmTarget objects; generate translates that representation into IDE files or Makefiles (L105-L135).

Source claim: the implementation is object-oriented C++ with inheritance and design patterns; a lex/yacc parser handles the language, and generated parser files are checked into the Source directory because lex/yacc may be unavailable; cmCommand subclasses carry both implementation and documentation (L144-L180).

Source claim: IDE builds delegate file-level dependency tracking to the IDE, while Makefile builds rely on generated depend.make, flags.make, build.make and DependInfo.cmake files, recomputed when a header change may add a dependency (L186-L192).

Source claim: CTest and CPack share CMake's code base but are separate tools; CTest runs add_test tests and can send results to CDash for distributed testing, while CPack builds an install tree and hands it to NSIS, RPM, Debian, tar or self-extracting packagers (L198-L204).

Source claim: the Qt and curses GUIs are editors of CMakeCache.txt with configure and generate buttons; new cache variables appear in red, and generate stays disabled until a configure pass creates no new variables (L210-L222).

Source claim: CMake development uses continuous integration with CTest and CDash, notifying developers of build errors, warnings and test failures; adding a platform is expected to come with a nightly dashboard client (L228-L234).

Source claim: lessons are a 2.6 policy system that warns but preserves old behavior, regret over the home-grown language with Lua named as the best alternative, plugin compatibility failures across 32/64-bit APIs, and a decision to reduce exposed APIs rather than become an embeddable library (L240-L264).

Inference: this is a participant history, and claims such as 'successfully building ITK from day one' (L240) and statements about developer preferences are not independently verified; the chapter reports no build-time, defect or adoption measurements.

notes: Source claim: the June 2010 Helios release covered over 39 projects and 490 committers from over 40 companies; Eclipse 1.0 appeared on 7 November 2001 as an extensible framework rather than a fixed tool set, with the SDK as its self-hosting proof of concept (L11-L14).

Source claim: early code derived from VisualAge for Java, and the first committers were paid employees of IBM subsidiary OTI; a vendor consortium (Borland, IBM, Merant, QNX, Rational, RedHat, SuSE, TogetherSoft) backed the effort before the 2004 Eclipse Foundation (L17-L20).

Source claim: a plugin is a JAR plus manifest, with its own class loader and explicit requires imports; extension points let outsiders contribute while exported packages define public API and everything else remains private (L44-L77).

Source claim: the runtime scans manifests at startup to build an in-memory extension registry, caches it to disk, and uses lazy activation so plugin classes load only when a contribution is used (L141-L187).

Source claim: the workbench is perspectives, views and editors built on SWT and JFace; SWT was chosen as a native toolkit after OTI's negative experience with Swing, a decision the chapter says split the Java community (L199-L220).

Source claim: JDT ships its own compiler, originally contributed from VisualAge Micro Edition, because tooling and extension points needed compiler internals; its incremental builder uses a resource delta and build state, recompiling dependents after structural changes (L280-L283). Source claim: PDE Build generated Ant scripts to assemble plugins because no existing Java build system understood the plugin format (L289).

Source claim: Eclipse 3.0's Equinox replaced the home-grown runtime with OSGi after rejecting JMX and Jakarta Avalon; OSGi was chosen for semantic versioning, explicit package exports, class loading and a broader community, with a compatibility layer for old plugins (L298-L313).

Source claim: the manifest gained Bundle-SymbolicName, Require-Bundle version ranges and a required execution environment; OSGi defines installed/resolved/starting/active/stopping/uninstalled states, four-part versions and dynamically registered services distinct from startup-registered extensions (L339-L360).
Source claim: community use of a platform subset produced RCP; bundles were split for that use case, with Mars Rover, Bioclipse and Dutch Railway cited as adopters (L389-L398).

Source claim: Update Manager could only update whole features and could not provision platform executables or license files, so p2 arrived in March 2008 with installable units, separated metadata/artifact repositories, profiles, director/planner/engine and touchpoints, enabling rollback and install-time constraint resolution (L404-L506).

Source claim: Eclipse 4.0 (July 2010 early adopter) pursued an EMF model workbench, CSS styling, hierarchical IEclipseContext dependency injection with JSR-330 annotations, and small application services ('the twenty things'), retaining a compatibility layer; the conclusion concedes the API grew too large and documentation was neglected (L512-L595).

sections: 8.3. File I/O Operations and Replica Management (L146)
notes: Source claim: HDFS is designed for very large data sets and high-bandwidth streaming; Yahoo! clusters span 40,000 servers holding 40 PB, with the largest cluster at 4,000 servers, and 100 other organizations report using Hadoop (L11-L20).

Source claim: metadata and application data are separated — a single NameNode per cluster holds namespace inodes and block locations while DataNodes store replicas; files are split into large blocks (typically 128 MB, three replicas), and replication substitutes for RAID (L23-L32).

Source claim: the namespace image lives in RAM, the persistent checkpoint is never updated in place, and a write-ahead journal records each transaction and is flushed and synced before acknowledgment; multiple transactions are batched to amortize the sync, and redundant copies sit on independent volumes and remote NFS (L38-L47).

Source claim: each DataNode replica is two local files (data plus metadata/checksums/generation stamp); a handshake checks namespace ID and software version, storage IDs survive restarts, block reports arrive hourly, and 3-second heartbeats carry commands because the NameNode never initiates connections (L53-L77).

Source claim: reads ask the NameNode for block locations sorted by topology distance and fall back to the next replica on failure; writes use a single-writer lease, a node-to-node packet pipeline, and an optional hflush for visibility guarantees (L89-L179).

Source claim: checksums are computed by the writer, stored beside each block, and verified by readers and by each DataNode's block scanner; corrupt replicas are not deleted until good copies reach the replication factor (L173-L179, L245-L251).

Source claim: default placement puts the first replica on the writer's node and the next two on different nodes in another rack, with later replicas random under one-per-node and two-per-rack limits; pipeline order follows proximity (L194-L209).

Source claim: replication management prioritizes blocks with one replica, avoids reducing rack diversity, and treats a single-rack block as mis-replicated; the balancer moves replicas between utilization extremes while preserving replica and rack counts, and DistCp copies data as a MapReduce job (L215-L263).

Source claim: example 4,000-node clusters have 11 PB raw storage (3.7 PB usable at three replicas), about 65 million files and 80 million blocks; 0.8% of nodes fail monthly, re-replication of a node's 60,000 replicas takes about two minutes, the scanner finds about 20 bad replicas per fortnight, and a full power-on restart loses a handful of blocks (L269-L290).

Source claim: sharing features include POSIX-like permissions without execute bits or sticky bits, Kerberos-based credentials, space and namespace quotas, and HAR archives; NameNode heap limits namespace and storage scale, so federation introduces independent namespaces sharing Block Pools, with client-side mount tables for a unified view (L296-L320).

Source claim: the authors attribute success to a small team, a simple architecture of replicated blocks, periodic block reports and central metadata, and avoiding full POSIX semantics; in-memory metadata avoids complex locking but caps scale, Java's object overhead and GC hurt the NameNode while avoiding pointer bugs, and failover remained manual when the chapter was written (L326-L329).

Inference: this is a vendor experience report from Yahoo!; the durability probabilities, failure rates and cluster statistics are operational recollections rather than a reproducible experiment, and the chapter dates to roughly 2010-2011.

sections: 11.1. A Quick Introduction to Classical Compiler Design (L23)
11.4.1. LLVM IR is a Complete Code Representation (L219)
11.4.2. LLVM is a Collection of Libraries (L231)
11.5. Design of the Retargetable LLVM Code Generator (L282)
11.6. Interesting Capabilities Provided by a Modular Design (L338)
11.6.1. Choosing When and Where Each Phase Runs (L344)
11.6.3. Automatic Test Case Reduction with BugPoint (L396)
notes: Source claim: LLVM began in December 2000 as reusable libraries with well-defined interfaces, in contrast to monolithic language implementations; the chapter presents broad reuse across static and JIT-compiled languages and special-purpose products, including OpenCL, as the outcome (L11-L20).

Source claim: the classical three-phase compiler separates a language-specific front end, a target-independent optimizer and a target-specific back end; this yields N+M rather than N*M implementations, widens the contributor community and lets front-end and back-end specialists work separately (L26-L53).

Source claim: the chapter evaluates prior reuse strategies — JVM/.NET bytecode forces JIT, GC and a particular object model, C-as-backend breaks exception handling, debugging and tail calls, and GCC remains monolithic with global state, layering problems and leaky abstractions (L59-L74).

Source claim: LLVM IR is a typed, RISC-like, three-address virtual instruction set with infinite named temporaries, defined in three isomorphic forms (textual .ll, in-memory structures, binary bitcode), with llvm-as and llvm-dis converting between text and bitcode (L80-L136).

Source claim: most optimizations follow pattern-match, safety-check, transform; SimplifySubInst implements X-0, X-X and (X*2)-X via C++ template matchers, and a dispatcher calls per-opcode helpers from passes that replace all uses with the simplified value (L142-L207).

Source claim: LLVM IR is the only optimizer interface and is self-contained, so a front end can emit text and pipe it through any optimizer/codegen sequence; GCC's GIMPLE is not self-contained because debug info and operands reach back to the source-level tree (L213-L228).

Source claim: LLVM is a set of libraries, not a monolithic compiler; each pass is a C++ class with a create function, passes live in archive libraries, and only referenced passes are linked, while PassManager satisfies declared dependencies; clients choose pass order and policy and may add language-specific passes (L234-L279).

Source claim: the code generator decomposes into instruction selection, register allocation, scheduling, layout and assembly emission, with per-target overrides (x86 pressure scheduling and x87 stack pass, PowerPC latency scheduling, ARM constant pools); declarative .td files processed by tblgen generate selector, allocator, encoder/decoder and parser support from one instruction description (L285-L335).

Source claim: bitcode serialization enables link-time optimization (-flto/-O4) and install-time optimization; textual IR plus the modular optimizer enables single-pass regression tests with opt and FileCheck, and BugPoint automates test-case reduction and fault isolation for crashes and miscompilations (L347-L408).

Source claim: modularity began as self-defense against getting the design wrong, and LLVM accepts API-breaking changes while offering stable C wrappers and backward-compatible bitcode; remaining work includes subsetting the still-monolithic code generator and improving generated code, with LLDB cited as a reuse example and calcification as the risk (L414-L426).
Inference: the author is LLVM's founder; the comparisons with GCC and claims about adoption, code quality and productivity are advocacy and recollection, not measurements reported in this chapter.
