No privileges on publications; cross-publication exposure of filtered or partial data (L18)
pg_create_subscription plus CREATE privilege to create a subscription (L20)
Apply process session privileges; per-table SET ROLE to the table owner (L22)
run_as_owner = true: no user switching and its privilege-escalation risk (L24)

notes: Source claim (L8): the replication connection role must have the REPLICATION attribute or be a superuser. If the role lacks SUPERUSER and BYPASSRLS, publisher row security policies can execute; a role that does not trust all table owners can pass options=-crow_security=off, after which an owner-added row security policy makes replication halt rather than execute the policy. Access must be allowed in pg_hba.conf and the role needs LOGIN.

Source claim (L10): the output plugin used by the replication connection must be included in output_plugin_libraries; subscriptions use pgoutput. Superusers may modify the trusted list per connection with options=-coutput_plugin_libraries=...
Source claim (L12, L14): copying initial table data requires SELECT on a published table (or superuser), and creating a publication requires CREATE privilege in the database.

Source claim (L16): adding tables to a publication requires ownership of those tables; adding all tables in a schema, or creating a publication that automatically publishes all tables or all tables in a schema, requires superuser.

Source claim (L18): there are currently no privileges on publications; any subscription able to connect can access any publication. Hiding information with row filters, column lists or partial table inclusion can be defeated by other publications in the same database exposing the same information; publication privileges might be added in the future.
Source claim (L20): creating a subscription requires the privileges of the pg_create_subscription role and CREATE privilege on the database.

Source claim (L22): the apply process runs at session level with the subscription owner's privileges, but switches to the table owner for insert, update, delete or truncate on each table; the subscription owner therefore needs SET ROLE to every role that owns a replicated table.

Source claim (L24): with run_as_owner = true there is no user switching; all operations use the subscription owner's permissions, which then only needs SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on the target table. However, any owner of a table receiving replication can execute arbitrary code with the subscription owner's privileges, for example by attaching a trigger, so the page says to avoid this setting unless user security within the database is unimportant.

Source claim (L26, L28): publisher privileges are checked once at the start of a replication connection and not re-checked per change record; subscriber-side subscription owner privileges are re-checked for each transaction. If ownership changes concurrently while a transaction is being applied, the current transaction continues under the old owner's privileges.

Inference: the asymmetric check timing means publisher-side grants revoked mid-stream are not re-evaluated per record, while subscriber-side ownership changes can affect later transactions but not an in-flight one.
Inference: run_as_owner shifts the trust boundary toward table owners, and the page frames that shift as a reason to avoid the setting rather than as an isolation model.

sections.heading: 29.2 Subscription: definition, topology and table matching (untitled introduction)
Example 1: connect = false, slot created manually
Example 2: connect = false with slot_name specified

notes: Source claim (L8-12): a subscription is the downstream side of logical replication; the node where it is defined is the subscriber; it defines a connection to another database plus one or more publications. The subscriber behaves like any PostgreSQL instance and can publish for others; a node may hold multiple subscriptions and a publisher-subscriber pair may have several, but care is required so subscribed publication objects do not overlap.

Source claim (L14-16): each subscription receives changes through one replication slot, with additional slots possibly needed for initial synchronization of pre-existing table data and dropped when synchronization ends. A subscription can act as a synchronous-replication standby; the standby name defaults to the subscription name and can be overridden by application_name in the connection string.

Source claim (L18-22): pg_dump dumps subscriptions only for a superuser, otherwise warns and skips them because non-superusers cannot read all subscription information from pg_subscription. CREATE SUBSCRIPTION adds a subscription, ALTER SUBSCRIPTION stops/resumes it, DROP SUBSCRIPTION removes it; dropping and recreating loses synchronization information, so data must be resynchronized.

Source claim (L24-28): schema definitions are not replicated and published tables must already exist on the subscriber; only regular tables can be replication targets, not views. Tables are matched by fully qualified name and columns by name (order may differ); types may differ if the text representation converts, e.g. integer to bigint; extra subscriber columns receive their declared defaults; binary-format replication is more restrictive.

Source claim (L32-36): each active subscription receives changes from a remote slot; table synchronization slots are normally transient, created internally for initial synchronization and dropped automatically, with generated names 'pg_%u_sync_%u_%llu' (subscription oid, table relid, system identifier). Normally the remote slot is created with CREATE SUBSCRIPTION and dropped with DROP SUBSCRIPTION.

Source claim (L38-44): slot management can be separated from subscription lifecycle. Use create_slot = false when the remote slot already exists; connect = false when the remote host is unreachable or unclear (pg_dump does this), requiring a manually created slot before activation; disassociate the slot with ALTER SUBSCRIPTION when moving the subscriber or when the remote is unreachable at drop time. An unreachable remote's slot (and leftover table sync slots) must be dropped manually, because it would keep reserving WAL and could fill the disk.

Source claim (L48-83): the setup example creates three tables with primary keys, publications pub1 (t1), pub2 (t2, publish = 'truncate'), pub3a (t3, publish = 'truncate') and pub3b (t3, row filter e > 5); subscription sub3 subscribes to both pub3a and pub3b, and all subscriptions copy initial data by default.

Source claim (L85-111, L154-182): initial table copying ignores the publication's publish operations and row filters - t2 is copied despite its truncate-only publication, and t3 receives all three initial rows despite pub3b's filter. During subsequent replication the publish operations and filter apply: the later inserts leave t2 at three rows and deliver only e = 6 to t3, giving t3 rows 1, 2, 3 and 6.

Source claim (L186-257): deferred slot creation requires creating the slot on the publisher with pg_create_logical_replication_slot(<slot_name>, 'pgoutput'), then ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... ENABLE and REFRESH PUBLICATION on the subscriber. With connect = false the slot name defaults to the subscription name unless slot_name is given; with slot_name = NONE the subscription also needs enabled = false and create_slot = false, and is later bound with ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... SET (slot_name = 'myslot').

Inference (reader): the page documents an explicit asymmetry between the initial copy (not governed by publish or row filters) and streaming changes (governed by both), but does not explain how the copy is coordinated with the slot's consistent point or how concurrent writes during the copy are handled; this page alone cannot support a snapshot-consistency claim.

Inference (reader): the overlap caution at L12 is stated for multiple subscriptions between one publisher-subscriber pair, while the example's single subscription sub3 covers the same table t3 through two publications (L71, L81-83). The page does not say whether the caution extends to multiple publications on one subscription, so the example should not be generalized into permission for overlapping publications.

Scope and representation note: conflict handling, security, monitoring, row-filter syntax and slot monitoring are covered by other chapter sections and were not read here. The example prompts '/* pub # */' and '/* sub # */' plus the query-result tables are source content, while the preamble, heading anchor links and link titles are extractor markup; no site navigation or footer appears in the capture.

notes: Source claim (L8): migration of logical replication clusters is possible only when all members of the old logical replication clusters are version 17.0 or later.

Source claim (L12): pg_upgrade attempts to migrate logical slots, avoiding manual redefinition on the new publisher, but slot migration is supported only from 17.0 or later; logical slots on older clusters are silently ignored.
Source claim (L14): before upgrading a publisher cluster the subscription must be temporarily disabled with ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... DISABLE and re-enabled after the upgrade.

Source claim (L18-28): pg_upgrade requires the new cluster to have wal_level = logical; max_replication_slots at least the number of old slots; the old slots' output plugins installed in the new executable directory and listed in output_plugin_libraries; the old cluster to have replicated all transactions and logical decoding messages to subscribers; all old slots usable, worded as 'there are no slots whose pg_replication_slots.conflicting is not true' (L26); and no permanent logical slots in the new cluster, i.e. no slot with temporary = false. Reader gloss: the L26 wording reads inverted relative to 'must be usable'; the operative condition is presumably conflicting = false.

Source claim (L32): for subscribers, pg_upgrade attempts to migrate subscription dependencies, including table information in pg_subscription_rel and the subscription's replication origin, so logical replication can continue from where the old subscriber stopped; this is supported only from 17.0 or later, and dependencies on older clusters are silently ignored.

Source claim (L36-40): subscriber upgrade prerequisites are that every subscription table in the old subscriber is in state 'i' (initialize) or 'r' (ready), verifiable via pg_subscription_rel.srsubstate; that the replication origin entry for each subscription exists (pg_subscription and pg_replication_origin); and that max_active_replication_origins is at least the number of subscriptions in the old cluster.

Source claim (L44-56): while a subscriber is upgraded, writes can continue on the publisher and will be replicated once the subscriber upgrade completes; the chapter's restrictions (Section 29.8) and both publisher and subscriber prerequisites also apply. A Warning states that upgrading requires multiple steps on various nodes, that not all operations are transactional, and that base backups should be taken as described in Section 25.3.2.

Source claim (L66-115): two-node procedure - disable node2's subscription, stop node1, initialize the new instance, run pg_upgrade, start node1, stop node2, initialize, upgrade and start node2, create on node2 any tables created on node1 since step 1, enable the subscription, then REFRESH PUBLICATION. A Note says publisher-first is not mandatory and the same steps can be applied subscriber-first.

Source claim (L117-189): cascaded procedure - disable node2's subscription from node1, upgrade node1, disable node3's subscription from node2, upgrade node2, create missing tables and enable/refresh node2's subscription, then upgrade node3, create missing tables, enable and refresh node3's subscription.

Source claim (L191-248): circular two-node procedure - disable node2's subscription from node1, upgrade node1, enable that subscription, create on node1 the tables created on node2 since step 1, REFRESH node1's subscription to copy initial data from node2, disable node1's subscription from node2, upgrade node2, enable the node1 subscription, create missing tables on node2, and REFRESH node2's subscription to copy initial data from node1.

Inference (reader): the page describes an ordered, stateful migration that depends on pg_upgrade preserving slot and origin state; it gives no timing, lag, downtime or capacity figures, no procedure for an interrupted upgrade or a partial migration, and no downgrade or rollback path. The Warning implies recovery relies on the advised base backup, not on reversing the upgrade.

sections.heading: Range notation: worked examples and edge cases

notes: Source claim (lines 6-8): a shard is a subset of a keyspace; a keyspace always contains one or more shards; a shard typically contains one MySQL primary and potentially many MySQL replicas, which hold identical data apart from replication lag and can serve read-only traffic with eventual consistency, long-running analysis, and administrative tasks such as backup, restore and diff.

Source claim (line 10): an unsharded keyspace has exactly one shard, named '0' (sometimes '-') by convention; a sharded keyspace has N shards holding non-overlapping data, the shard count varies with use case and load, and some Vitess users run hundreds of shards in a keyspace.

Source claim (lines 12-19): shard names represent a range in unsigned integer space (left bound included, right bound excluded), are written in hexadecimal, are left-justified and right-padded with zeros; a '-' prefix means anything less than the right value, a '-' postfix means anything greater than or equal to the left value, and a plain '-' denotes the full keyrange.

Source claim (lines 21-27): '-80', '00-80', '0000-8000' and the sixteen-hex-digit form denote the same range; '80-FF' equals '8000-FF00', so 'FFFF' falls outside '80-FF'; consequently '80-' is not the same as '80-FF', and '80-' means anything greater than or equal to 0x80.

Source claim (line 29): an xxhash-type vindex produces an unsigned 64-bit integer, so every value below 0x8000000000000000 falls in shard '-80' and every value with the highest bit set belongs to shard '80-'.

Source claim (lines 31-35): the left-justified encoding permits keyspace IDs of arbitrary length with the most significant bits on the left; an md5 hash (16 bytes) can serve as a keyspace ID, and an arbitrary-length varbinary can be mapped as-is by the 'binary' vindex.

Source claim (lines 37-39): resharding changes the shard count on a live cluster by splitting shards into smaller pieces or merging neighbouring shards; source data is copied to destination shards, allowed to catch up on replication, compared against the original for integrity, live serving is shifted, and the source shards are deleted.

Inference (reader, not stated on the page): the page defines a shard simultaneously as a keyrange and as a MySQL replication group, but says nothing about where topology and routing metadata live, how the cutover in resharding is coordinated, or what read consistency holds across shards, so mechanism-level claims about those need other sources.

sections.heading: Overview: startup, SQL-to-KV path, ranges, consensus, storage

notes: Source claim (L7-L13): CockroachDB is described as a source-available database designed to be both scalable and consistent; the guide explains the inner workings of the `cockroach` process for serious users and enthusiasts, states that understanding the architecture is not required to use the product, and points to a free introductory course.

Source claim (L15-L23): the guide is organized by architecture layers and is meant to be read sequentially from this overview to the SQL layer; each layer's Overview section suffices for a high-level understanding while Components sections add technical detail for readers such as project contributors; the guide does not explain application development.

Source claim (L27-L35): stated goals are low-touch, highly automated operation and simple reasoning for two audiences; industry-leading consistency at scale through distributed transactions, without eventual-consistency or stale-read pain; always-on reads and writes on all nodes without conflicts; flexible deployment in any environment without platform or vendor lock-in; and familiar relational tooling such as SQL.

Source claim (L39-L57): a cluster starts with `cockroach start` carrying `--join` for all initial nodes plus a one-time `cockroach init`; clients use a PostgreSQL-compatible SQL API and may send statements to any node; nodes convert SQL RPCs into KV operations, data is algorithmically distributed into ranges, and each range is replicated to at least 3 nodes by default for survivability; requests a node cannot serve are forwarded; range changes commit through Raft consensus; the storage engine tracks timestamps and thereby supports the SQL standard `AS OF SYSTEM TIME` clause.

Source claim (L61-L73): the architecture is presented as five layers, each interacting with adjacent layers as relatively opaque services: (1) SQL translates queries to KV operations, (2) transaction layer allows atomic changes to multiple KV entries, (3) distribution layer presents replicated KV ranges as a single entity, (4) replication layer synchronously replicates ranges across nodes and enables consistent reads via consensus, (5) storage layer reads and writes KV data on disk. The native table retains all layer names and purpose cells.

Source claim (L77-L93): consistency means a transaction changes affected data only in allowed ways, used in both ACID and CAP senses but less formally than either; isolation is the degree to which a transaction may be affected by concurrent transactions, with `SERIALIZABLE` and `READ COMMITTED` offered; consensus is agreement on commit or abort, implemented with Raft, where a quorum of replica-holding nodes acknowledges a write and forward progress halts without consensus; replication requires writes to propagate to a quorum of copies before commit.

Source claim (L95-L106): a transaction is a set of operations satisfying ACID; contention appears as lock contention (another concurrent or recent transaction writes the same data) or as a serialization conflict (no serializable ordering among currently executing transactions); CockroachDB retries automatically where possible, otherwise emits a transaction retry error that requires a client under `SERIALIZABLE` isolation to retry; the page advises reducing contention in the first place.

Source claim (L108-L114): multi-active availability is a consensus-based notion in which each node handles reads and writes for a per-range subset, contrasted with active-passive (one active node receives all traffic) and active-active (all nodes accept requests but reads are typically not both current and fast); a SQL user is an identity that authenticates by username/password, SSO or certificate and is distinct from a CockroachDB Cloud organization user.

notes: Source claim (L4): sharding distributes data across multiple machines; MongoDB uses it for deployments with very large data sets and high-throughput operations.
Source claim (L6-L8): an Important callout states the feature is not currently supported on Atlas Infinite clusters during public preview.

Source claim (L10-L18): single-server capacity is limited by CPU for high query rates and by disk I/O when the working set exceeds RAM; vertical scaling enlarges one server and meets a practical maximum, while horizontal scaling adds servers, can cost less than high-end hardware and increases infrastructure and maintenance complexity; Atlas deployments can shard in the UI.

Source claim (L24-L42): a sharded cluster has shards (each holding a subset of data and deployed as a replica set), mongos query routers between clients and the cluster, and config servers storing metadata and settings (a replica set, CSRS); since MongoDB 8.0 a config server can be a config shard that also stores application data; MongoDB shards at collection level, distributing collection data across shards.

Source claim (L44-L77): the shard key is one or more document fields used to distribute a collection; missing key fields are treated as null for distribution but not for routing; the key is chosen when sharding; since 5.0 a collection can be resharded with a new key; a key can be refined by adding suffix fields; a document's key value can be updated unless the key is the immutable _id. The same section adds that sharding a populated collection requires an index whose prefix is the shard key; for an empty collection MongoDB creates a supporting index when no suitable one exists; the key and its backing index constrain the sharding strategy.

Source claim (L79-L89): sharded data is partitioned into chunks with an inclusive lower and exclusive upper shard-key bound; a background balancer migrates ranges across shards to even out distribution.

Source claim (L91-L107): sharding spreads read and write load so both can scale horizontally by adding shards; queries containing the shard key or a compound-key prefix can be targeted to specific shards, which is generally more efficient than broadcast; storage capacity grows with added shards; config servers and shards deployed as replica sets raise availability, and if one or more shard replica sets are unavailable the cluster can still serve partial reads and writes against available shards.

Source claim (L109-L139): sharded infrastructure requires planning and maintenance; resharding later is possible but key choice should avoid scalability and performance problems; queries lacking the shard key or prefix cause broadcast scatter/gather that can be long running; since 5.1 a Cluster Wide Write Concern must be set when starting, restarting or adding a shard with sh.addShard(), and an unset CWWC with default write concern {w:1} makes the shard fail to start or be added; resharding marks the donor range for removal by a slow, resource-intensive range deleter, one chunk migration per shard at a time; since 8.0 sh.shardAndDistributeCollection() wraps shardCollection and reshardCollection to rebalance without waiting for the balancer.

Source claim (L141-L161): a database can mix sharded and unsharded collections; unsharded collections may live on any shard but cannot span shards; clients must connect to mongos for all collections and must not connect directly to a shard; since 8.3 DDL and applyOps on sharded clusters run only on mongos (temporarily unavailable during Atlas replica-set-to-sharded transitions); since 8.0 only certain commands run on sharded-cluster nodes, otherwise an error is returned, and unsupported commands require mongos or the maintenance-only directShardOperations role.

Source claim (L163-L189): MongoDB supports hashed and ranged sharding; hashed sharding computes a hash of the key and gives more even distribution, especially for monotonic keys, but makes range queries more likely to broadcast; ranged sharding keeps close key values together and enables targeted routing, but poorly chosen keys can skew data and create bottlenecks.

Source claim (L191-L249): zones associate shard-key ranges with shards for locality across data centers, each range inclusive of its lower and exclusive of its upper bound, and zone ranges must use shard-key fields including a compound prefix; sharding a collection with a default collation requires a shard-key-prefix index with the simple collation, while queries keep the collection's default collation unless overridden; change streams work on replica sets and sharded clusters; multi-document transactions span shards, and reads at local read concern can observe one write of a committed multi-shard transaction before another; Learn More points to an e-book chapter on aggregations.

Source claim: the black-box template lists Purpose/Responsibility, Interface(s) including qualities and performance characteristics, optional Quality-/Performance characteristics, optional directory/file location, optional fulfilled requirements for traceability, and optional open issues, problems or risks; it may be written as a table or text.

sections.heading: Best Practices for Data Modeling in MongoDB (intro)
sections.summary: Frames the page as guidance for balancing performance and adaptability while ensuring consistency and integrity, and links to schema planning and design-pattern pages.

sections.heading: Plan Your Schema Early and Iterate
sections.summary: Plan early to avoid growth problems; the flexible schema supports iteration, but large production schemas remain difficult to modify.

sections.heading: Modify Your Data Model
sections.summary: Learning-platform example: lessons start embedded; when videos, quizzes, assignments and links arrive, split them into a `lessons` collection linked by reference IDs.

sections.heading: Link Related Data
sections.summary: Embed or reference; a scenario table maps embedding to has-a, co-read, co-updated and co-archived data and referencing to high cardinality, duplication cost, size/bandwidth pressure, unbounded arrays, different write times and parent-independent children.

sections.heading: Duplicate Data
sections.summary: Duplication trades cheaper reads (no joins) for update logic; classifies duplicates as immutable, temporal, staleness-sensitive and staleness-tolerant.

sections.heading: Enforce Data Consistency
sections.summary: Consistency options are embedding related data, transactions and Atlas Database Triggers, with a pointer to the data-consistency page for tradeoffs.

sections.heading: Enforce Schema with Validation Rules
sections.summary: Validation suits established applications with a defined structure; rules need not cover every field; examples cover an events date type, a store card-type set and a students positive GPA.

sections.heading: Index Commonly Queried Fields
sections.summary: Index frequently queried, filtered, sorted or joined fields; claimed benefits include faster reads and sorting plus `$lookup`/`$group` optimization; costs include at least 8 kB per index, write overhead, disk and memory.

sections.heading: Additional Considerations
sections.summary: Introduces atomicity, lifecycle, hardware and small-document considerations alongside read and write operations.

sections.heading: Atomicity
sections.summary: Writes are atomic per document; embedded data gets atomic multi-subdocument updates, references need separate operations, and multi-document transactions exist but cost more than single-document writes.

sections.heading: Data Lifecycle Management
sections.summary: TTL collections expire documents after a period (30-minute login-session example); capped collections provide FIFO insertion-order management.

sections.heading: Hardware Constraints
sections.summary: Design for available RAM and keep the working set small by returning only relevant fields.

sections.heading: Small Documents
sections.summary: Per-document overhead matters for tiny documents; suggests explicit `_id`, shorter field names (9 bytes saved in the example) and embedding, while noting field-name shortening does not shrink indexes.

sections.heading: Learn More
sections.summary: Points to a MongoDB University data-modeling course.

sections.heading: Archive Pattern (intro)
sections.summary: Keeping old, infrequently accessed data in the same database can hurt performance; archive old data to separate storage instead.

sections.heading: About this Task
sections.summary: Three storage options - external file storage such as Amazon S3, a separate cheaper cluster, or a separate collection on the same cluster - with external file storage recommended 'in most cases' for cost and performance.

sections.heading: Tips for Data Archival
sections.summary: Archive documents should be embedded rather than referenced, carry the document age in a single field, use a 'keep forever' sentinel for records that must not move, and can use Atlas Online Archive.

sections.heading: Scenario
sections.summary: An e-commerce store archives sales older than five years from the active sales collection to a separate collection.

sections.heading: Steps
sections.summary: Step 1 inserts four sales (two dated 2018 and 2017), step 2 computes a rolling five-year cutoff, copies older documents with $match + $merge into archived_sales, then deletes them from sales.

sections.heading: Results
sections.summary: After the script, db.sales.find() returns only the two 2025 sales and db.archived_sales.find() returns the two older sales.

sections.heading: Learn More
sections.summary: Links to Atlas Online Archive, Designing Your Schema and Schema Design Anti-Patterns.

notes: Source claim (L5): storing the oldest data in the same database as recent data can negatively impact performance, especially when old data does not need frequent access; the recommended alternative is to archive old data and move it to a separate storage location.

Source claim (L9-L17): archived data can go to external file storage such as Amazon S3, a separate cheaper cluster, or a separate collection on the same cluster; external file storage is called the best option in terms of cost and performance 'in most cases', with a separate cluster or collection as fallback.

Source claim (L21-L29): archive documents should use an embedded data model rather than references because all relevant components of archived data must come from the same time; the document's age should live in a single field; records that must never expire or move should carry a sentinel such as 'keep forever'; Atlas Online Archive moves infrequently accessed data to a managed read-only Federated Database Instance on cloud object storage.

Source claim (L33, L40-L105): the scenario archives sales older than five years; the inserted sample contains four sales, of which the 2018-11-20 and 2017-06-15 records are older than five years and the two 2025 records are not.

Source claim (L115-L147): the script derives the cutoff at run time (now minus five years), uses an aggregation with $match on date < cutoff and $merge into test.archived_sales keyed on _id, then calls deleteMany with the same predicate inside a try/catch that prints the error.

Source claim (L151-L243): the listed results show the active sales collection holding only the two recent documents and archived_sales holding the two old documents, with the same field shapes and ObjectIds as inserted.

Inference (reader): copy-then-delete is two separate operations with no transaction, checkpoint or verification between them. A failure after $merge but before or during deleteMany leaves the same sale in both collections; the try/catch prints the error but does not retry, reconcile or confirm the archive, and the page does not discuss concurrent writes during the copy.

Inference (reader): the single age field is a schema convention, not an enforced rule. The page does not show an index on the age field, and a 'keep forever' string in a field otherwise compared as a date would not satisfy the numeric date comparison used by the script; the page does not reconcile the sentinel with the $lt predicate.

Inference (reader): the 'best option in terms of cost and performance' recommendation is unquantified; the page gives no storage price, retrieval latency, data volume, retention horizon or restore path, and the Atlas Online Archive bullet is a pointer to a vendor service rather than a measured comparison.

The six fenced JavaScript blocks use three-space indentation inside the numbered steps, preserved in the capture.

sections.heading: Single Collection Pattern (intro)
sections.summary: An array of references groups related documents of different types into one collection, aimed at many-to-many relationships with one copy of the data; characteristics and high-velocity/low-latency fit.

sections.heading: About this Task
sections.summary: Student/class status application: frequently updated class fields, no duplication across students, students and classes kept as separate entities in one collection.

sections.heading: Example
sections.summary: Class and student documents each carry a links array of {target, doc_type}; a compound index on links.target and links.doc_type supports two single-collection queries without joins.

sections.heading: Learn More
sections.summary: Links to Data Modeling in MongoDB and Best Practices for Data Modeling in MongoDB.

No site navigation, footer, cookie/consent, language or breadcrumb chrome is present in the native Markdown capture.
notes: Source claim (L5): the pattern uses an array of references to group related documents of different types into a single collection; it is called especially useful for many-to-many relationships with only one copy of the data, reducing duplication where duplication cost is a concern.

Source claim (L9-L13): the defining characteristics are that all frequently accessed documents are stored together in one collection, relationships are stored as pointers or structures inside each document, and relationships are mapped by indexes on the field or array so related documents are retrieved in one query without database join operations.

Source claim (L15): the pattern is suggested for systems with high-velocity operations, low-latency requirements and frequent writes; breaking a document into smaller parts instead of large embedded documents is said to allow smaller writes and improve performance.

Source claim (L19): the example is a student/class status application where fields such as current_topic, upcoming_session_summary and next_class_time are updated frequently; students and classes stay separate document entities in one collection to avoid duplicating class information per student.

Source claim (L23, L27-L63): the class document (for example _id CS101-001) embeds instructor and schedule, carries the mutable class fields, and has a links array containing a self-link to the class plus student targets, abbreviated with an ellipsis at L60.

Source claim (L69-L92): the student document (for example _id S12345) carries name, major and semester, a registered_classes array of {course_id, class_instance_id, class_name}, and a links array containing class targets plus a self-link.

Source claim (L95-L111): the page indexes { "links.target": 1, "links.doc_type": 1 } and shows two queries - find({ "links.target": "S12345" }) for a student and their classes, and find({ "doc_type": "student", "links.target": "CS101-001" }) for a class's registered students - both described as requiring no join.

Inference (reader): the 'one copy of the data' statement holds for the canonical class document but not for every field. Each student repeats class_name and course_id inside registered_classes, and every relationship is recorded from both ends in links plus a self-link, so the pattern removes joins and duplicated class bodies rather than all duplication.

Inference (reader): the links arrays are reciprocal edges maintained by the application. The page does not say how the two sides are kept consistent (no transaction, update ordering or repair job), nor how array growth is bounded when a class or a student accumulates many links.

Inference (reader): 'improve performance' and 'smaller write operations' are qualitative. The page shows no explain output, index or document size, or measurement, so neither the join-free retrieval nor the write-size benefit is evidenced by a plan or benchmark.

Representation note: the ellipsis inside the links array (L60) means the class document is abbreviated and not literally runnable; the collection name students_classes appears only in the createIndex and find commands and the page does not show its creation. The five code blocks are preserved verbatim.
Scope note: sharding, transactions, consistency of reciprocal links, pagination of links, and comparison with the embedding or subset patterns are not discussed on this page.

notes: [source] full text search identifies natural-language documents that satisfy a query and optionally sorts them by relevance; query and similarity are application-dependent, with the simplest case being a word set and query-word frequency.

[source] `~`, `~*`, `LIKE` and `ILIKE` are criticized for lacking linguistic support (derived forms such as satisfies/satisfy), result ranking, and index support, which makes them slow on large collections.

[source] indexing preprocesses documents in three stages: parsing into classified tokens, converting tokens into normalized lexemes (case folding, suffix removal, stop-word elimination) via dictionaries, and storing a search-optimized representation with optional positions for proximity ranking.

[source] `tsvector` stores preprocessed documents and `tsquery` processed queries; `@@` returns true on a match regardless of operand order, and the `text @@ tsquery` / `text @@ text` variants avoid explicit casts.

[source] tsquery supports `&`, `|`, `!`, `<->` (FOLLOWED BY) and `<N>` distance forms; `<0>` requires the same word, precedence is `|`, then `&`, then `<->`, then `!` from loosest to tightest, and parentheses override it.
[source] `'fat cats ate fat rats'::tsvector` does not normalize, so it fails `to_tsquery('fat & rat')`, whereas `to_tsvector(...)` succeeds; tsvector elements are assumed already-normalized lexemes.
[source] `phraseto_tsquery('the cats ate the rats')` renders as `'cat' <-> 'ate' <2> 'rat'`, encoding the stop-word gap as a position distance.

[source] NOT and AND/OR change meaning inside FOLLOWED BY: `!x <-> y` matches y when it is not immediately preceded by x, and `(x & y) <-> z` requires x and y at the same position before z, unlike `x <-> z & y <-> z`.

[source] configurations control stop words, synonyms and parsing; `default_text_search_config` can be set per cluster, database or session, and each configuration-dependent function accepts an optional `regconfig` argument; parsers, dictionaries, templates and configurations are the four object types, with parsers/templates requiring C and superuser privileges to install.

[source] omitting configuration arguments makes the functions use `default_text_search_config`.

[source] unindexed scans are characterized as too slow for most applications except occasional ad-hoc searches; practical use usually requires an index.

[source] a GIN expression index is built on `to_tsvector('english', body)`; expression indexes must use the two-argument form because index contents must not depend on `default_text_search_config`, otherwise entries could mix configurations and dump/restore could not reconstruct them.
[source] a query uses the expression index only if it repeats the same two-argument expression and configuration name.
[source] an expression index can take the configuration from another column (`to_tsvector(config_name, body)`), supporting mixed-language collections when queries match, and can concatenate columns.

[source] alternatively, a stored generated `tsvector` column built with `coalesce` can be GIN-indexed; queries then need not name the configuration and avoid re-running `to_tsvector`, which the text says is faster (more important for GiST than GIN); the expression index is simpler and uses less disk because the tsvector is not stored.

The page example turns 'a fat cat sat on a mat - it ate a fat rats' into 'ate':9 'cat':3 'fat':2,11 'mat':7 'rat':12 'sat':4: a/on/it are dropped as stop words, rats becomes rat, and '-' is ignored.

Source claim (L25): the parser assigns each token a type; for each token, the dictionary list selected for that type is consulted and the first dictionary that recognizes the token emits normalized lexemes. Stop words and unrecognized tokens are ignored. Parser, dictionaries and indexed token types are determined by the text search configuration; many configurations can coexist and predefined language configurations exist, with english used in the example.

Source claim (L27-37): setweight labels a tsvector's entries with weight A, B, C or D, typically to mark document parts such as title versus body for later ranking. Because to_tsvector(NULL) returns NULL, coalesce is recommended; the page's structured-document pattern labels title A, keyword B, abstract C and body D, then merges the vectors with the || operator.

Source claim (L41-75): four query constructors are provided: to_tsquery (more features, less forgiving), plainto_tsquery, phraseto_tsquery and websearch_to_tsquery (a simplified, web-search-like syntax). to_tsquery requires single tokens separated by & (AND), | (OR), ! (NOT) or <-> (FOLLOWED BY), possibly parenthesized; it normalizes tokens to lexemes and discards stop words, accepts weight labels such as :AB and prefix '*', and accepts single-quoted phrases for thesaurus rules. Tokens not separated by an operator raise a syntax error.

Source claim (L77-95): plainto_tsquery parses and normalizes text much as to_tsvector does, then inserts & between surviving words. It does not recognize tsquery operators, weight labels or prefix-match labels: 'The Fat & Rats:C' becomes 'fat' & 'rat' & 'c', and all input punctuation is discarded.

Source claim (L97-113): phraseto_tsquery behaves like plainto_tsquery but inserts <-> between surviving words, and accounts for stop words with <N> operators rather than discarding them; it therefore checks lexeme order, not just presence. Like plainto_tsquery, it does not recognize tsquery operators, weight labels or prefix labels.

Source claim (L114-158): websearch_to_tsquery accepts simple unformatted text, recognizes some operators and never raises syntax errors, so raw user input can be used. Unquoted text becomes &-separated terms, quoted text becomes <->-separated terms, the word 'or' becomes |, a dash becomes ! and other punctuation is ignored. Examples include '"supernovae stars" -crab' -> 'supernova' <-> 'star' & !'crab' and a malformed string reduced to 'dummi' & 'queri'.

Source claim (L162-202): ts_rank ranks by frequency of matching lexemes; ts_rank_cd computes cover density as described by Clarke, Cormack and Tudhope (Information Processing and Management, 1999), taking proximity into account. ts_rank_cd needs positional information, ignores stripped lexemes and returns zero when no unstripped lexemes remain. The optional weight array is ordered {D-weight, C-weight, B-weight, A-weight} and defaults to {0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 1.0}.

Source claim (L184-244): both ranking functions accept an integer normalization bit mask: 0 ignores length, 1 divides by 1+log(length), 2 by length, 4 by mean harmonic distance between extents (ts_rank_cd only), 8 by unique-word count, 16 by 1+log(unique-word count) and 32 by rank+1; multiple bits apply in the listed order. The functions use no global information, so no fair 1%/100% normalization is possible; option 32 maps ranks into 0..1 cosmetically without changing order. Ranking can be expensive because it consults each matching document's tsvector and may be I/O bound.

Source claim (L250-274): ts_headline accepts a document, query and optional comma-separated options, returns an excerpt, selects fragments using the query, and highlights all query words even where positional restrictions do not match. Options are MaxWords/MinWords (defaults 35/15), ShortWord (3), HighlightAll (false), MaxFragments (0 selects single-excerpt mode), StartSel/StopSel (/) and FragmentDelimiter (' ... '); option names are case-insensitive and string values with spaces or commas must be double-quoted.

Source claim (L268-270, L274, L302): ts_headline output is not guaranteed safe for direct inclusion in web pages. With HighlightAll false some simple XML tags are removed, but not all HTML markup, so this is not an effective XSS defense; input markup should be removed or output sanitized. Non-fragment mode chooses one best match; fragment mode splits matches into at most MaxWords words, prefers more query words and stretches around them; with no match the first MinWords words are shown. ts_headline reads the original document rather than a tsvector summary, so it can be slow.

Inference (reader, not stated on the page): the page defines mechanisms and tunable options but reports no latency, index-size or relevance-quality measurements; its performance statements are qualitative ('can be slow', 'can be expensive'), so it supports no benchmark claim.

sections.heading: 12.9 Preferred Index Types for Text Search (whole page, no subsections)

notes: Source claim (L8): two index kinds can speed up full text searches, GIN and GiST. Indexes are not mandatory for full text searching, but an index is usually desirable when a column is searched regularly.

Source claim (L10-16): CREATE INDEX ... USING GIN (column) creates a GIN-based index and the column must be of tsvector type. CREATE INDEX ... USING GIST (column [ { DEFAULT | tsvector_ops } (siglen = number) ]) creates a GiST-based index; the column may be tsvector or tsquery, and the optional integer siglen sets signature length in bytes.

Source claim (L18): GIN indexes are the preferred text search index type. As inverted indexes they hold an entry per lexeme with a compressed list of matching locations; a multi-word search can find the first match and then use the index to remove rows lacking additional words. GIN stores only tsvector lexemes, not weight labels, so a query involving weights requires a table row recheck.

Source claim (L20): a GiST index is lossy and can produce false matches, requiring a check of the actual table row, which PostgreSQL performs automatically when needed. Each document is represented by a fixed-length signature; siglen controls its length, the default is 124 bytes and the maximum is 2024 bytes. Each word is hashed to one bit in an n-bit string and the bits are OR-ed into a document signature; two words hashing to the same bit produce a false match. If all query words have matches (real or false), the row is retrieved. Longer signatures make searches more precise (smaller index fraction, fewer heap pages) at the cost of a larger index.
Source claim (L22): a GiST index can be covering by using the INCLUDE clause; included columns may have data types without any GiST operator class, and included attributes are stored uncompressed.

Source claim (L24): lossiness degrades performance through unnecessary table-row fetches that turn out to be false matches. Because random access to table records is slow, this limits GiST's usefulness; false-match likelihood depends on factors including the number of unique words, so dictionaries that reduce that number are recommended.
Source claim (L26): GIN index build time can often be improved by increasing maintenance_work_mem, while GiST index build time is not sensitive to that parameter.

Source claim (L28): partitioning large collections and using GIN and GiST indexes properly allows very fast searches with online update. Partitioning can be done at database level with table inheritance, or by distributing documents over servers and collecting external search results, for example through Foreign Data access; the latter is possible because ranking functions use only local information.

Inference (reader, not stated on the page): the page gives no latency or index-size measurements and no workload-specific rule for choosing GiST over GIN beyond calling GIN preferred; its quantitative details are the signature limits (124 default, 2024 maximum) and the qualitative build-time sensitivity to maintenance_work_mem.

notes: Source claim (L14-17): tsvector || tsvector concatenates two vectors, retaining lexemes, positions and weight labels; positions in the right-hand vector are offset by the largest position in the left-hand vector. The result is nearly equivalent to running to_tsvector on the concatenated text, but not exactly, because stop words removed from the end of the left argument would have shifted right-hand positions under textual concatenation. Vector concatenation allows different configurations for different document sections, and setweight must be applied before concatenation to give sections different weights.

Source claim (L19-22): setweight(vector, weight) returns a copy in which every position is labeled A, B, C or D; D is the default for new vectors and is not shown on output. Labels are retained when vectors are concatenated, so ranking can weight document parts differently. Weight labels apply to positions, not lexemes; setweight does nothing to a vector stripped of positions.

Source claim (L24-30): length(vector) returns the number of lexemes stored in the vector. strip(vector) returns the same lexemes without position or weight information; the result is usually much smaller but less useful, relevance ranking works less well, and the <-> (FOLLOWED BY) tsquery operator never matches stripped input because distance between lexeme occurrences cannot be determined. A full function list is in Table 9.43.

Source claim (L36-58): tsquery && tsquery returns the AND combination, || the OR combination, !! the negation, and tsquery <-> tsquery a FOLLOWED BY match (example: 'fat' <-> ('cat' | 'rat')). tsquery_phrase(query1, query2 [, distance]) searches for the second query exactly distance lexemes after the first using the <N> operator (example: 'fat' <10> 'cat').

Source claim (L59-83): numnode(query) returns the number of nodes (lexemes plus operators), useful to tell whether a query is meaningful (>0) or contains only stop words (0); examples return 0 with a NOTICE for 'the any' and 3 for 'foo & bar'. querytree(query) returns the portion usable for an index search, useful for detecting unindexable queries such as stop-word-only or fully negated ones; 'defined' yields 'defin' and '!defined' yields T.

Source claim (L87-107): the ts_rewrite family finds occurrences of a target subquery in a tsquery and replaces each with a substitute subquery, a tsquery-specific substring replacement. A collection of target/substitute rules can expand synonyms (new york, big apple, nyc, gotham) or narrow a topic. This overlaps thesaurus dictionaries (Section 12.6.4), but rewrite rules can be changed on the fly without reindexing whereas updating a thesaurus requires reindexing. The three-argument form applies one rule ('a & b', target 'a', substitute 'c' -> 'b' & 'c'); the select form requires two tsquery columns and applies each row's target/substitute, with application order mattering, so ORDER BY an ordering key is advised.

Source claim (L109-136): a table-driven example expands supernovae to supernovae|sn, producing 'crab' & ('supernova' | 'sn'); updating the aliases table changes the rules without reindexing. Rewriting can be slow with many rules because every rule is checked for a match; the containment operators can filter obvious non-candidates, e.g. WHERE ''a & b''::tsquery @> t.

Source claim (L140-175): a note states that the trigger method in this section has been obsoleted by stored generated columns (Section 12.2.2). For a separate tsvector column, a trigger is needed to update it when content columns change; two built-in trigger functions exist: tsvector_update_trigger(tsvector_column_name, config_name, text_column_name [, ...]) and tsvector_update_trigger_column(tsvector_column_name, config_column_name, text_column_name [, ...]). The first argument is the tsvector column, the second is a schema-qualified configuration name (so search_path changes do not alter behavior) or a regconfig column for per-row configuration, and remaining arguments are text/varchar/char columns included in the given order; NULL values are skipped while other columns are still indexed.

Source claim (L177-191): the built-in triggers treat all input columns alike; weighting title differently from body requires a custom trigger, illustrated with a PL/pgSQL function applying setweight A to title and D to body. The page stresses specifying the configuration name explicitly inside triggers so column contents are unaffected by changes to default_text_search_config, which could otherwise change search results after a dump and restore.

Source claim (L195-221): ts_stat(sqlquery text, [weights text,] OUT word text, OUT ndoc integer, OUT nentry integer) returns setof record. sqlquery must return a single tsvector column; ts_stat executes it and returns one row per distinct lexeme with word, ndoc (number of documents/tsvectors containing it) and nentry (total occurrences). Supplying weights counts only occurrences with those weights; examples select the ten most frequent words overall and with weights 'ab'.

sections.heading: 12.6 Dictionaries - role, contract and ordering
sections.summary: Dictionaries remove stop words and normalize tokens into lexemes, which also shrinks the tsvector and is claimed to improve performance (L8); four normalization examples including URL canonicalization and decimal truncation (L10-L24); return contract - lexeme array, TSL_FILTER single lexeme, empty array for a stop word, NULL for an unknown token (L26-L34); predefined dictionaries and templates, and a configuration binding a parser to per-token-type dictionary lists where the first non-NULL result wins (L36-L38); narrow-to-general ordering rule with the astro_en example (L40-L43); a filtering dictionary may sit anywhere except last, e.g. unaccent (L45).

sections.heading: 12.6.1 Stop Words
sections.summary: Stop words have no discrimination value but keep their positions in the tsvector: 'in the list of stop words' yields 'list':3 'stop':5 'word':6, and ts_rank_cd reads 0.05 versus 0.1 without them (L49-L66); ispell normalizes before the stop-word check while Snowball checks stop words first (L68).

sections.heading: 12.6.2 Simple Dictionary
sections.summary: Lowercases the token and checks a stop-word file; ts_lexize returns {yes} for 'YeS' and {} for 'The'; Accept=false returns NULL for non-stop words so a later dictionary can decide, and then a following dictionary is required (L72-L108).

sections.heading: 12.6.2 Cautions - file encoding and reload
sections.summary: Configuration files must be stored in UTF-8 and are translated to the database encoding when read (L112); a session reads a file once, so changed contents need ALTER TEXT SEARCH DICTIONARY, possibly a dummy update (L116).

sections.heading: 12.6.3 Synonym Dictionary
sections.summary: Replaces a word with a synonym and does not support phrases; the Paris/paris entry stops english_stem reducing Paris to pari (L120-L139); SYNONYMS names a .syn file under $SHAREDIR/tsearch_data and CaseSensitive defaults to false (L141-L143); a trailing asterisk marks a prefix, ignored by to_tsvector but emitted as ':*' by to_tsquery (L145-L174), shown with a psql transcript (L176-L186).

sections.heading: 12.6.4 Thesaurus Dictionary
sections.summary: Extends the synonym dictionary with phrase support; the file maps 'sample word(s) : indexed word(s)' with colon as delimiter (L192-L199); exactly one subdictionary normalizes input and a leading asterisk skips it for an indexed word (L201); the longest match wins and ties use the last definition (L203); '?' stands for any subdictionary stop word (L205-L209); phrase handling needs parser interaction and correct token-type assignment (L211); parameter changes require reindexing (L215).

sections.heading: 12.6.4.1 Thesaurus Configuration
sections.summary: CREATE TEXT SEARCH DICTIONARY with TEMPLATE=thesaurus, DictFile=mythesaurus and Dictionary=pg_catalog.english_stem, the .ths file under $SHAREDIR/tsearch_data, then ALTER MAPPING FOR asciiword, asciihword, hword_asciipart (L221-L239).

sections.heading: 12.6.4.2 Thesaurus Example
sections.summary: thesaurus_astro maps 'supernovae stars' to sn; plainto_tsquery('supernova star') returns 'sn' after the stemmer removes the e and s, and repeating the phrase on the right-hand side yields 'sn' & 'supernova' & 'star' (L245-L288).

sections.heading: 12.6.5 Ispell Dictionary
sections.summary: Morphological normalization of related word forms and possessives; the distribution ships no dictionary files, and Ispell, MySpell and Hunspell formats are accepted (L292-L294); preparation converts .aff/.dic to .affix/.dict, optional iconv to UTF-8, copy to $SHAREDIR/tsearch_data, then CREATE TEXT SEARCH DICTIONARY with DictFile/AffFile/Stopwords (L296-L312); .affix flag and .dict 'basic_form/affix_class_name' formats (L316-L343); compound splitting via 'compoundwords controlled' with Norwegian ts_lexize output (L345-L354); Hunspell PFX/SFX layout and field list (L356-L383); MySpell has no compounds and PostgreSQL implements only basic Hunspell compound operations (L385-L387).

sections.heading: 12.6.6 Snowball Dictionary
sections.summary: Porter-derived stemmers per language; Language is required and StopWords optional; the built-in english_stem definition is shown; because it recognizes everything it must be placed last (L391-L401).

notes: Source claim: a dictionary returns an array of lexemes for a known token, a single lexeme with TSL_FILTER to replace the token for later dictionaries, an empty array for a stop word, or NULL when it does not recognize the token (L26-L34).

Source claim: normally the first dictionary returning non-NULL determines the result and later dictionaries are not consulted, while a filtering dictionary's replacement is passed onward; hence the narrow-to-general ordering rule (L38-L45).

Source claim: stop words keep their positions in the tsvector, so ranking changes; the page shows 'list':3 'stop':5 'word':6 and ts_rank_cd 0.05 against 0.1 for the same words without stop words (L49-L66).
Source claim: ispell dictionaries normalize before checking the stop-word list while Snowball stemmers check the stop-word list first (L68).
Source claim: dictionary configuration files must be UTF-8 and are read once per session; reloading requires ALTER TEXT SEARCH DICTIONARY, which may be a dummy update (L112-L116).

Source claim: a thesaurus uses exactly one subdictionary, takes the longest phrase match, breaks ties with the last definition, and needs reindexing after parameter changes, unlike small stop-word edits for most other dictionary types (L201-L215).
Source claim: MySpell does not support compound words, Hunspell does, and PostgreSQL implements only the basic Hunspell compound operations (L385-L387).

sections.heading: 12.5 Parsers - role
sections.summary: Parsers split raw document text into tokens and identify each token's parser-defined type; a parser does not modify text, it only identifies plausible word boundaries; because of that limited scope custom parsers are needed less often than custom dictionaries, and one built-in parser covers a wide range.

sections.heading: Built-in parser and token-type count
sections.summary: The built-in parser is pg_catalog.default and recognizes 23 token types, tabulated in Table 12.1.

sections.heading: Table 12.1 Default Parser's Token Types
sections.summary: 23 rows, each with description and example: asciiword, word, numword, asciihword, hword, numhword, hword_asciipart, hword_part, hword_numpart, email, protocol, url, host, url_path, file, sfloat, float, int, uint, version, tag, entity, blank (L16-L38).

sections.heading: Note - locale, email and tag limits
sections.summary: A letter is defined by the database locale, specifically lc_ctype, and ASCII-only words are a separate token type that in most European languages can be treated like word (L44); email allows only period, dash and underscore beyond alphanumerics in user names, not all RFC 5322 characters (L46); tag accepts only names starting with an ASCII letter, underscore or colon and containing letters, digits, hyphens, underscores, periods and colons, and also covers XML comments and declarations, including anything starting with <?x and ending with > (L48).

sections.heading: Overlapping tokens example
sections.summary: foo-bar-beta1 is reported as numhword plus hword_asciipart foo and bar and hword_numpart beta1, with '-' as blank; the overlap is stated to be desirable so both the compound and its components can match (L50-L62).

sections.heading: URL token example
sections.summary: http://example.com/stuff/index.html is reported as protocol, url, host and url_path tokens, with the url_path shown in the context of a URL (L64-L70).

notes: Source claim: parsers only break text into tokens and label token types; they do not modify the text, and the type set is defined by the parser itself (L8).
Source claim: PostgreSQL provides just one built-in parser, pg_catalog.default, and the page argues custom parsers are less necessary than custom dictionaries (L8-L10).
Source claim: the default parser recognizes 23 token types; Table 12.1 lists 23 rows, so the stated count and the table agree (L10-L38).
Source claim: token-type recognition of letters depends on lc_ctype, and asciiword versus word separation exists because distinguishing basic ASCII words is sometimes useful (L44).
Source claim: the email token type supports only period, dash and underscore as non-alphanumerics in user names, so not all RFC 5322 addresses are parsed as email (L46).
Source claim: the tag token type covers a restricted name grammar plus XML comments and XML declarations, which also captures anything starting with <?x and ending with > (L48).
Source claim: one text span can yield overlapping tokens; the hyphenated example emits the whole word and each component, which is presented as desirable for matching compounds and parts (L50-L62).
Observation: the page names token types but never shows how they map to dictionaries; that binding is performed in configurations and is outside this unit.

Inference: no parsing cost, token-count or latency figures appear, and the two examples are the only behavioural evidence; the claim that one parser fits a wide range of applications is not qualified by corpus type.
Observation: both result tables are publisher ts_debug output, not executed during this read; neither ends with a psql row-count line, and the URL table stops at url_path.

sections.heading: 12.7 Configuration Example - framing
sections.summary: A configuration specifies everything needed to turn a document into a tsvector, namely the parser and the dictionaries that map tokens to lexemes; every to_tsvector or to_tsquery call needs one, and default_text_search_config supplies the default, set in postgresql.conf or per session with SET (L8); several predefined configurations exist, custom ones are easy, and SQL plus psql commands (Section 12.10) manage and display them (L10).

sections.heading: Duplicate english and add a synonym list
sections.summary: CREATE TEXT SEARCH CONFIGURATION public.pg (COPY = pg_catalog.english); the $SHAREDIR/tsearch_data/pg_dict.syn file maps postgres, pgsql and postgresql to pg; CREATE TEXT SEARCH DICTIONARY pg_dict (TEMPLATE = synonym, SYNONYMS = pg_dict).

sections.heading: Register the Ispell dictionary
sections.summary: CREATE TEXT SEARCH DICTIONARY english_ispell (TEMPLATE = ispell, DictFile = english, AffFile = english, StopWords = english), with the note that it has its own configuration files.

sections.heading: Map token types to the dictionary chain
sections.summary: ALTER TEXT SEARCH CONFIGURATION pg ALTER MAPPING FOR asciiword, asciihword, hword_asciipart, word, hword, hword_part WITH pg_dict, english_ispell, english_stem.

sections.heading: Drop unneeded token types
sections.summary: ALTER MAPPING ... DROP MAPPING FOR email, url, url_path, sfloat, float, described as choosing not to index or search token types the built-in configuration handles.

sections.heading: Test with ts_debug
sections.summary: SELECT * FROM ts_debug('public.pg', ...) over a sample sentence; the call is shown without its result set.

sections.heading: Activate and verify
sections.summary: \dF lists public.pg in schema public; SET default_text_search_config = 'public.pg' followed by SHOW confirming public.pg.

notes: [source] 12.8 introduces `ts_debug` for testing a whole configuration, with optional `config regconfig` defaulting to `default_text_search_config`; it returns one row per parser token with alias, description, token, candidate dictionaries, recognizing dictionary and lexemes.
[source] Output semantics: a `NULL` dictionary means no dictionary recognized the token; `{}` lexemes means a stop word; `NULL` lexemes means no recognition.
[source] The first example shows `a` and `on` as stop words (`{}`) and the hyphen as a `blank` token with no dictionaries.

[source] The extended example creates `public.english` from `pg_catalog.english`, adds `english_ispell`, and maps `asciiword`; `Brightest` becomes `{bright}` via ispell while `supernovaes` falls through to `english_stem` and becomes `{supernova}`.
[source] `The` is recognized by `english_ispell` as a stop word and not indexed; spaces are discarded because the configuration provides no dictionaries for them.
[source] `ts_parse` returns `tokid` and token text; the example `123 - a number` yields tokid 22 for `123`, 12 for blanks/hyphen, and 1 for `a`/`number`.
[source] `ts_token_type` returns the integer `tokid`, alias and description for each of the 23 default token types.

[source] `ts_lexize` returns lexemes for known tokens, `{}` for stop words, `NULL` for unknown tokens; it treats input as one token, so the thesaurus phrase `supernovae stars` returns NULL and `plainto_tsquery`/`to_tsvector` are recommended for phrase tests (the example `plainto_tsquery` result is `'sn'`).
[inference] The three subsections form a layered diagnostic path: configuration mapping, parser segmentation, then dictionary normalization.

sections.heading: OpenTelemetry Collector as a sidecar / host agent
OpenTelemetry Collector as a remote cluster

notes: Jaeger v2 is described as a single binary that can be configured into roles: collector, query, ingester, all-in-one, and agent (L8-L16).
The agent role is configured but not recommended; the page points to the standard OpenTelemetry Collector instead because other telemetry types likely need processing (L16).

Collector/query separation is presented as allowing independent read and write scaling plus different access and security policies; both all-in-one and collector/query are said to scale horizontally when an external backend is used (L18).

All-in-one with in-memory storage is positioned for development/testing because data is lost on restart; all-in-one with Badger may be used in production only for modest volumes and cannot scale horizontally (L20).

Direct-to-storage: collectors write straight to the backend, which must absorb average and peak traffic; an in-memory queue smooths short peaks, while a sustained spike may cause dropped data if storage cannot keep up (L24-L28).

Kafka variant: collectors use Kafka exporters, a separate ingester reads Kafka and writes storage, and multiple ingesters partition the load automatically; an ingester is described as a collector with a Kafka receiver instead of RPC receivers (L32-L34).

The Jaeger binary is built on the OpenTelemetry Collector framework and mixes official upstream components, contrib components, and Jaeger-specific components; custom distributions can be built with ocb (L68-L76).
Jaeger-specific components named: Storage Extension (shared storage hub), Storage Exporter, Query Extension, Adaptive Sampling Processor, and Remote Sampling Extension (L80-L90).

An OpenTelemetry Collector may precede Jaeger as sidecar/host agent or as a remote cluster; the stated sidecar benefit is simpler SDK endpoint configuration and local enrichment, with an extra marshal/unmarshal layer as the cost (L38-L56).
Remote-cluster placement adds sharding capability, exemplified by tail-based sampling, again at the cost of an extra marshaling layer (L58-L66).

sections.heading: Index-header file layout (fenced diagram, not a heading)

notes: Source claim (L86): to query series inside blocks held in object storage, the store-gateway must obtain information about each block index; it builds an index-header for every block and stores it on local disk.

Source claim (L90): downloading only those sections is described as computationally easy, so the index-header is not uploaded to object storage; when no local copy exists, store-gateway instances rebuild it from the block index, including the same instance after a rolling update that leaves no persistent disk.
Source claim (L94-97): format version 1 is a subset of the block index holding the Symbol Table, used to unintern string values, and the Posting Offset Table, used to look up postings.

Source claim (L99, L103-116): the file is terminated by a table of contents that is the entry point into the index; the layout orders magic 0xBAAAD792 (4 bytes), version 1 (1 byte), index version 2 (1 byte), an 8-byte posting-offset-table field, then the Symbol Table, the Posting Offset Table and the TOC.
Source claim (L110, L112): both tables are marked as exact copies of the corresponding sections of the original index, so the header duplicates index metadata rather than transforming it.
Inference: the design assumes re-reading a few index byte ranges is cheap relative to fetching a whole block index, but the page reports no sizes, latency figures, request counts or measurements.
Inference: no eviction, capacity, concurrency or invalidation policy for local index-header copies is stated; the only lifecycle rule given is rebuild-on-miss.

sections.heading: How it’s used by the querier
How it’s used by the store-gateway
Footnote 1: definition of 'almost up-to-date' (not a heading)

notes: Source claim (L86): the bucket index is a per-tenant file listing blocks and block deletion marks, stored in backend object storage, periodically updated by the compactor, and used by queriers, store-gateways and rulers in internal operational mode to discover blocks.

Source claim (L90): those components need an almost up-to-date view of the bucket; without the index they must periodically scan it for new blocks uploaded by ingesters or compactors and for blocks deleted or marked for deletion.

Source claim (L92-98): with the index enabled, querier, store-gateway and ruler look up the per-tenant index instead of issuing `list objects` calls; the listed benefits are fewer object-storage API calls, no list-objects calls from querier and store-gateway, and a querier that is ready immediately after startup without an initial bucket scan.

Source claim (L102-109): `bucket-index.json.gz` contains `blocks` (complete blocks, including those marked for deletion; partial blocks excluded), `block_deletion_marks`, and `updated_at`, a Unix timestamp in seconds recording the last write.
Source claim (L113): the compactor periodically scans the bucket and uploads an updated index; the cadence is set by `-compactor.cleanup-interval`.

Source claim (L115): the index is built and updated even when `-blocks-storage.bucket-store.bucket-index.enabled=false`, so it exists if an operator enables the feature on a live cluster; the page calls the resulting overhead not significant.

Source claim (L119-121): querier and ruler download the index lazily on first need and cache it in memory; the file is small, so lazy download is said not to affect first-query performance materially, and the optional metadata cache shares it for a short time across queriers and rulers.

Source claim (L125-132): an in-memory background process refreshes the cached index at `-blocks-storage.bucket-store.sync-interval`; a failed download is itself cached for `-blocks-storage.bucket-store.bucket-index.update-on-error-interval` so the backend is not flooded with retries.

Source claim (L134): an index unused for `-blocks-storage.bucket-store.bucket-index.idle-timeout` is dropped from memory and stops being refreshed, which the page ties to tenants being resharded when shuffle sharding is enabled.

Source claim (L136): at query time staleness is judged from `updated_at`; a query fails if the index is older than `-blocks-storage.bucket-store.bucket-index.max-stale-period`, a circuit breaker against partial results from a stale view.

Source claim (L140, L144): the store-gateway fetches the index at startup and periodically for each tenant in its shard and treats it as the source of truth for blocks and deletion marks; 'almost up-to-date' means lagging by less than `-compactor.deletion-delay`, because fetching an already-deleted block fails the query.

Inference: the page states that index maintenance overhead is not significant but supplies no measurement, and it does not describe how an index replacement is made atomic or how readers handle a partially visible update; the workflow diagram at L123 is an image reference that was not inspected.

Source claim: five components join dedicated rings - ingesters (shard and replicate series), compactors (compaction jobs), store-gateways (blocks from long-term storage), optional rulers (rule groups) and optional alertmanagers (tenants) (L23-L27).

Source claim: the ring models data space as 32-bit unsigned integers; an instance owns token ranges and handles a hashed value when it owns the smallest registered token greater than the lookup token, wrapping after (2^32)-1 (L29-L33).

Source claim: on join or leave only a bounded portion moves, stated as 'on average, only n/m tokens move, where n is the total number of tokens (32-bit unsigned integer) and m is the number of instances' (L35). Source claim (ingest storage, write): distributors hash each series with fnv32a, look up the partitions ring and write to the matching Kafka partition; Kafka handles replication; ingesters own partitions, one partition per ingester but multiple ingesters may own one partition for HA; a write succeeds when all series are committed to Kafka (L48-L67).

Source claim (ingest storage, read): the querier resolves the partitions ring, then the ingesters ring, then contacts one healthy owner per partition; consistency is stated as a quorum of 1, so each partition is queried only once (L73-L79).

Source claim (partition lifecycle): partitions are not live components but are managed by ingesters - created Pending, promoted Active after a grace period once they have an owner, moved Inactive for read-only draining, then removed when the last owner leaves; the rollout operator drives downscale through two ingester endpoints (L83-L113).

Source claim (classic write): the distributor replicates each series to the next RF-1 ingesters clockwise, RF defaults to 3, and a write succeeds at a quorum of 2 of 3; the worked example hashes a series to token 3, maps it to ingester #2 (token 4) among tokens 2/4/6/9 and replicates to ingesters #3 and #4 (L126-L143).

sections.heading: Grafana Mimir memberlist and gossip protocol
How memberlist propagates hash ring changes

notes: Source claim (l.86): Memberlist is a Go library that manages cluster membership, node failure detection and message passing over a gossip protocol; it is described as eventually consistent, with network partitions only partially tolerated by trying to reach potentially dead nodes through multiple routes.
Source claim (l.88): by default Grafana Mimir uses memberlist to implement a key-value store that shares the hash-ring data structures between instances; this page names no alternative KV backend.

Source claim (l.90): each instance maintains a copy of the hash rings, updates the ring locally, propagates the change with memberlist, and merges locally generated with received updates to form the ring state it acts on.

Source claim (l.92): configuration is delegated to the separate 'configuring hash rings' page; this page documents only the memberlist gossip and pull-push options and gives no defaults, fan-out sizes or interval values.
Source claim (l.96-99): two propagation techniques are named — propagating only the differences introduced in recent changes, and propagating the full hash-ring data structure.

Source claim (l.101): every -memberlist.gossip-interval an instance randomly selects a subset of cluster instances bounded by -memberlist.gossip-nodes and sends only the latest changes; this is called frequent and the primary propagation path.

Source claim (l.103): every -memberlist.pullpush-interval an instance randomly selects one peer and transfers the full KV-store content including all rings, unless the interval is zero; afterwards both instances have the same content; it is costlier, performed less often, and reconciles rings periodically.

Inference: convergence is bounded by interval configuration and random peer selection, not by a stated guarantee; the page supplies no convergence time, gossip fan-out default, message size, failure-detector timeout or partition-healing behaviour, so quantitative membership claims should not be attributed to it.

Inference: 'eventually consistent' and 'partially tolerated' partitions (l.86, l.88) combined with merge-on-instance ring state imply interval-scale staleness can reach a reader, but the page never states what correctness an operator should assume during a partition — an explicit unknown.
