sections.heading: Known differences compared to Prometheus' engine
Binary operations that produce no series

notes: Source claim (l.86): the Mimir Query Engine (MQE) is an alternative to Prometheus' query engine and can be used in queriers to evaluate PromQL queries.

Source claim (l.88): MQE is said to produce equivalent results, generally use less memory and CPU, and evaluate queries at least as fast; it supports all stable PromQL features and transparently falls back to Prometheus' engine for unsupported features.
Source claim (l.92): MQE is enabled by default; it is disabled with -querier.query-engine=prometheus or the equivalent YAML option.

Source claim (l.96-100): fallback is enabled by default; -querier.enable-query-engine-fallback=false disables it and then an unsupported query fails; the X-Mimir-Force-Prometheus-Engine: true header forces Prometheus' engine for a supported query, but only while fallback is enabled.

Source claim (l.104-106): MQE can enforce a per-query memory limit, estimating memory for the final result and intermediate calculations and stopping the query with err-mimir-max-estimated-memory-consumption-per-query when the estimate exceeds the configured limit.

Source claim (l.108-114): the estimate covers samples held in memory (raw samples decoded from chunks, intermediates and final result, plus some other large intermediate sources) and has stated limitations — series-label memory is ignored, chunks currently in memory are ignored while chunk count/bytes limits still apply, and native-histogram memory is assumed rather than calculated.

Source claim (l.116-118): no limit is enforced by default; -querier.max-estimated-memory-consumption-per-query or YAML sets the tenant-wide default, a per-tenant max_estimated_memory_consumption_per_query overrides it, 0 disables it, and the limit never applies when MQE is disabled, the query falls back, or the query uses Prometheus' engine.

Source claim (l.126-129): MQE uses series labels to skip binary-operation work — it skips both sides when the operation provably yields no series (foo{env="test"} / bar{env="prod"}), and skips unmatched series on one side (env="3" ignored in the on(env) example).

Source claim (l.131-137): consequences are an 'aborted stream because query was cancelled' log line when streaming from ingesters/store-gateways stops early, missing counter annotations that Prometheus emits during series-data evaluation, and missing 'found duplicate series for the match group' errors when one side of a match group is empty.

Source claim (l.141): topk and bottomk results differ from Prometheus' engine when different series tie on sample values; Prometheus is described as non-deterministic across evaluations, and MQE's implementation differs as a result.

Inference: the page asserts 'equivalent results' (l.88) while documenting known differences (l.120-141); it supplies no numbers for estimate accuracy, estimator overhead, query-latency deltas or fallback frequency, so its memory and speed adjectives are unquantified claims.

sections.heading: Example 3: Query with two shardable portions

notes: Source claim (L86): sharding runs one query across multiple machines by breaking the dataset into shards; each shard is queried by a partial query, the query-frontend distributes partial queries to different queriers in parallel, and the frontend aggregates the results into the full result.
Source claim (L88): query sharding is applied only to the query and query_range HTTP APIs, not to other read endpoints.

Source claim (L92-L94): shardability is partial. Associative aggregations (sum, min, max, count, avg) are shardable; absent, absent_over_time, histogram_quantile, sort_desc and sort are named as not shardable. A non-shardable full query can still have shardable inner parts.

Source claim (L96, L98-L174): partial queries are distinguished by a __query_shard__ label selector (1_of_4 ... 4_of_4 for a shard count of 4) and a concat() annotation marks where the frontend concatenates or merges partial results; the three worked examples rewrite sum(rate(...)), histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by(le) ...) and a two-legged ratio.
Source claim (L180): sharding is opt-in via -query-frontend.parallelize-shardable-queries=true.

Source claim (L182): each shardable portion becomes -query-frontend.query-sharding-total-shards partial queries, and multiple inner portions multiply, which the page says can lead to a query explosion; the default hard limit is 128 partial queries per input query, adjustable with -query-frontend.query-sharding-max-sharded-queries.

Source claim (L184-L186): with -query-frontend.split-queries-by-interval enabled, the cap applies to the time-split-then-shard-split total; the worked example is a cap of 128 over an 8-day range at 24h splitting giving 16 partial queries per day.

Source claim (L188-L194): once sharding is enabled in a microservices deployment the frontends do the aggregation, so PromQL engine parameters must also be set on the frontend: -querier.max-concurrent, -querier.timeout, -querier.max-samples, -querier.default-evaluation-interval, -querier.lookback-delta.

Source claim (L198-L200): parallelization lowers query processing time but raises load on queriers and their stores (ingesters for recent data, store-gateways for historic data) and on the chunk and index caching layer; the page recommends raising frontend parallelism by multiplying -querier.max-query-parallelism by -query-frontend.query-sharding-total-shards.

Source claim (L204-L210, labelled experimental): cardinality estimation uses series counts observed in previous executions of the same query over similar ranges; it is enabled with -query-frontend.query-sharding-target-series-per-shard plus the query-frontend.results-cache.* flags, which are needed even when results caching is off because estimates live in that cache. The target is advisory and can be exceeded when cardinality changes quickly; estimates only ever reduce shards and never raise them above the configured cap. Histogram cortex_query_frontend_cardinality_estimation_difference tracks estimate error.

Source claim (L216-L253): verification uses the frontend query-statistics field sharded_queries - 0 means unshardable or disabled, equal to the shard count means one leg, a multiple means several legs (32 with shard count 16 = two legs) - plus the ratio of cortex_frontend_query_sharding_rewrites_succeeded_total to _attempted_total and the histogram cortex_frontend_sharded_queries_per_query.

Inference: the page describes the mechanism, flags and load direction but gives no latency, throughput or cost figures, so it supports qualitative fan-out claims only; the one diagram (L176) is an image URL and its drawn flow was not read.

sections.heading: Disaster Recovery of Workloads on AWS: Recovery in the Cloud
High availability is not disaster recovery
Business impact analysis and risk assessment
Disaster recovery is different in the cloud
Disaster recovery options in the cloud

notes: Source claim (L8): "Disaster recovery is the process of preparing for and recovering from a disaster"; an event that prevents a workload or system from fulfilling its business objectives in its primary deployed location is considered a disaster; the paper states it offers approaches to mitigate risks and meet the workload's RTO and RPO.

Source claim (L26, L45): disaster recovery measures objectives for one-time events, whereas availability measures mean values over a period of time (MTBF/MTTR, "nines"); disaster recovery focuses on disasters while availability focuses on smaller disruptions, and both should be part of a resiliency strategy.

Source claim (L87-92): disasters are grouped as natural, technical and human; each also has a geographical impact from local to global; the paper illustrates multi-AZ mitigation for local flooding against a cross-Region failover for an attack on production data.

Source claim (L99, L103): availability focuses on components whereas disaster recovery focuses on discrete copies of the entire workload; because continuous replication can propagate deletion or corruption, a point-in-time backup is also required as part of a disaster recovery strategy.

Source claim (L110, L115, L121): the disaster recovery plan should be a subset of the business continuity plan; a business impact analysis should quantify impact and tolerable data loss; for low-probability disasters an informed decision to have no disaster recovery strategy is described as valid.

Source claim (L137, L146, L156): RTO is the maximum acceptable delay between interruption of service and restoration of service; RPO is the maximum acceptable amount of time since the last data recovery point; if the recovery strategy costs more than the failure, it should not be put in place unless a secondary driver such as regulatory requirements exists.

Source claim (L194, L205): strategies are categorized into four approaches; active/passive keeps a passive site that does not serve traffic until a failover event is triggered; failover should use only data-plane operations because data planes typically have higher availability design goals than control planes.

Source claim (L210, L220, L231, L248): backup and restore must redeploy infrastructure, configuration and code, preferably with infrastructure as code; backup frequency determines the achievable recovery point; continuous replication has near-zero backup time but may not protect against corruption or malicious deletion; data restore from backup is a control-plane operation and can be scheduled as an SDK-driven recurring job.

Source claim (L261, L287, L291, L295, L299): pilot light keeps data replication and core infrastructure running while application servers are switched off; promoting a non-Aurora RDS read replica takes a few minutes while Aurora global database promotion is stated as under one minute, and Aurora can monitor RPO lag; automatic failover on health checks should be used with caution because a false alarm also incurs loss, so manual initiation with automated steps is often used; Route 53 ARC is described as a data-plane switch while weighted routing is a control-plane operation; CloudFront origin failover operates per request.

Source claim (L321, L330, L335, L342): pilot light cannot process requests without additional action whereas warm standby can serve reduced capacity immediately; Auto Scaling is a control-plane dependency accepted as a trade-off, with a statically provisioned "hot standby" alternative; multi-site active/active serves traffic from all Regions and has no failover event, targets near-zero recovery time, but data corruption still implies a non-zero recovery point, and recovery time for a data disaster is always greater than zero.

Source claim (L351-354): active/active write designs are described as write-global (one write Region, another promoted on failure), write-local (DynamoDB global tables with last-writer-wins reconciliation) and write-partitioned (partition-key routing; bidirectional S3 replication between two Regions), with stated consistency and replication caveats.

Source claim (L363, L368, L385, L389): with a one-hour RTO, detection, notification, escalation, evaluation, declaration and recovery must all fit inside the hour; detection, notification, escalation, discovery and declaration must be factored into objectives; "the only error recovery that works is the path you test frequently"; configuration drift at the DR Region (AMIs, service quotas, AWS Config) must be managed.

notes: Source claim (28): Sigstore is an open-source project for software supply-chain security that signs and verifies release files, container images, binaries and SBOMs; signatures use ephemeral signing keys so keys need not be managed, and signing events are recorded in a tamper-resistant public log.

Source claim (30): the project is backed by the OpenSSF under the Linux Foundation with contributions from Google, Red Hat, Chainguard, GitHub and Purdue University, is 100% open source and free, and the community operates a public-good non-profit service. This is a project-provenance statement, not evidence of governance, funding or support terms.

Source claim (34-40): unsigned software is exposed to typosquatting, compromised hosting sites and tampering after publication; digital signatures let consumers trace an artifact to its source and detect alteration after signing.

Source claim (44-50): traditional keypair signing has identity, key-management and revocation weaknesses — verifying who signed, protecting the private key while publishing the public key, and redistributing keys after compromise.

Source claim (52-56): Sigstore moves from key-based to identity-based signing; with full capabilities an artifact is signed by Cosign, associated with an identity through Fulcio, and witnessed by recording signing information in Rekor.

Source claim (58-62): 'keyless' or 'ephemeral key' signing means verification relies on the transparency log rather than keys; the claimed benefits are convenience (no key management or rotation), CI automation and public auditability.

Source claim (66-68): the client creates a keypair and sends a certificate signing request to Fulcio with the public key and a verifiable OIDC token carrying an email, service account or CI workflow identity; Fulcio verifies the token and issues a short-lived certificate bound to that identity and public key; services never obtain the private key, which is discarded after a single signing.

Source claim (70): the artifact digest, signature and certificate are persisted in Rekor, described as an immutable append-only ledger; identity owners can monitor use of their identity and a downloader can confirm the certificate was valid at signing time.

Source claim (72): verification checks the artifact signature with the certificate's public key, checks the certificate identity against an expected identity, validates the certificate signature against Sigstore's root of trust, and verifies proof of inclusion in Rekor.

Inference: 'keyless' here means no long-lived signing keys, not the absence of cryptography — a short-lived X.509 certificate and a root of trust still mediate verification; the page does not specify certificate lifetime, clock-skew tolerance, revocation or log-availability behavior.

notes: Source claim (L3-5): a search request is routed to a replica of a shard; the chosen replica acts as an aggregator, issuing internal requests to randomly chosen replicas of every shard, coordinating responses and issuing follow-up requests for facet refinement or stored fields before constructing the final response.

Source claim (L9-11): each node load balances reads across replicas; an external load balancer or a ZooKeeper-aware client (CloudSolrClient) may be needed; a node can answer as long as it reaches at least one replica of every shard, or of every relevant shard when shards or _route_ limit the query, and more replicas increase the chance of answering during node failures.

Source claim (L15-17, L37): a node returns results even when it cannot communicate with ZooKeeper, which is preferred for fault tolerance but may return stale or incorrect results if the collection structure changed without the node being informed; every response carries a zkConnected header, and shards.tolerant=requireZkConnected makes such requests fail instead.

Source claim (L41-47): shards.tolerant defaults to false and fails the request when a queried shard is unavailable; true may return partial results and sets a partialResults flag when results do not cover all appropriate shards; requireZkConnected also fails when shards are unavailable; shards.info can be requested for fine-grained details.

Source claim (L72-76): distrib.singlePass=true fetches all requested stored fields from each shard in the first phase, avoiding a second request; it can be faster for a few small fields and slower for large or numerous fields; faceting and similar features may still make additional network requests.

Source claim (L86-114): a query without a shards parameter covers all shards; the shards parameter may list logical shard IDs, explicit replica addresses, or pipe-separated alternative replicas per shard, and specifying replicas limits the request to those replicas.

Source claim (L118-122): shards.preference sorts available replicas within each shard by property order (primary, secondary, and so on); in single-shard collections it is supported only through SolrJ clients.

Source claim (L126-148, L160-166): preference properties include replica.type (PULL, TLOG, NRT), replica.location (local, host, host-prefix), replica.base, replica.leader and node.sysprop; local and host can avoid network transfer but can create hotspots unless requests are load balanced across all nodes hosting replicas; a non-leader TLOG replica behaves like a PULL replica for search yet captures updates so it can replace a lost leader.

Source claim (L210-216): the collection parameter runs a query over several collections; _route_ maps a route key (multiple comma-separated keys allowed) to the shards holding that key, with a trailing "!" shown in the example.

Source claim (L223-231): near real time means documents become searchable soon after indexing; hard and soft commits control durability and visibility, typically hard commits with openSearcher=false and soft commits for visibility; background tasks such as segment merging do not block updates; cache and autowarm settings matter at short commit intervals.

Source claim (L241-259): distributed IDF depends on document and term statistics that vary from node to node; statsCache implementations are LocalStatsCache (the default), ExactStatsCache, ExactSharedStatsCache and LRUStatsCache; distrib.statsCache defaults to true and can disable global statistic fetches for a query.

Source claim (L265-267): each shard serves top-level requests and makes sub-requests to other shards, so the HTTP thread pool must exceed the combined top-level and inter-shard requests; otherwise a distributed deadlock can occur, illustrated by two single-threaded shards blocking on each other's sub-requests.

notes: Source claim (L1-L17): a vector index speeds up vector search while payload indexes speed up filtering; indexes live in segments and exist independently, but their parameters are configured for the whole collection; the optimizer decides which segments get indexes. Payload indexes are built for a field and type, serve filtering conditions and estimate filter cardinality for query planning; supported types are keyword, integer, float, bool, geo, datetime, text and uuid, with version notes v1.4, v1.8 and v1.11.

Source claim (L18-L89): indexes can target nested fields via dot notation; open-ended keys should be reshaped; payload indexes should be created before ingestion because filter-aware HNSW edges are generated only after payload indexes exist, otherwise the HNSW index must be rebuilt. Strict mode with unindexed_filtering_retrieve=false rejects queries on unindexed fields, and Qdrant Cloud applies these settings by default.

Source claim (L90-L105): parameterized integer indexes expose lookup and range flags, both true by default; setting one false can reduce memory, but a range filter with range=false, or a match filter with lookup=false, may cause significant performance issues (table L99-L103).

Source claim (L213-L324): prefix matching for keyword indexes is available as of v1.19.0, adds prefix and substring support, is distinct from the full-text prefix tokenizer, matches byte-wise and case-sensitively, requires a rebuild when added to an existing index, and is rejected under strict mode without a prefix-enabled keyword index.

Source claim (L325-L541): payload indexes are always persisted; pinned is the default memory tier, while cached and cold trade memory for disk I/O. Tenant indexes (v1.11.0) structure storage per tenant, do not require non-overlapping tenants, and support keyword and uuid.

Source claim (L542-L823): principal indexes (v1.11.0) optimize storage for a primary filter field and support integer, float and datetime. Per-element indexes (v1.20.0) index each array element via nested, are limited to one array level, cannot also be tenant or principal, rebuild when nested changes, and change is_empty, full-text and BM25 behavior.

Source claim (L824-L1124): a full-text index makes string words searchable and supports filtering and BM25 ranking; phrase matching and BM25 scoring are independent. BM25 is available as of v1.20.0, scoring=true is a REST shorthand, text-processing settings apply to indexed text and queries, k and b are per-query, and scoring costs memory and disk but can be rebuilt from stored payload.

Source claim (L1125-L1533): tokenizers are word (default), whitespace, prefix, multilingual (charabia/vaporetto) and code (v1.20.0, splitting identifiers and camelCase and adding joined tokens); lowercasing is enabled by default, ASCII folding (v1.16.0) is opt-in, Snowball stemming is opt-in, and stopword removal is opt-in.
Source claim (L1534-L1861): phrase matching requires an additional data structure configured at index creation; the page's only instruction is to use the Phrase Match condition.

Source claim (L1862-L2086): Qdrant uses HNSW as its only dense vector index; HNSW is a multi-layer graph tuned by m, ef_construct and ef, with a YAML example giving m:16, ef_construct:100 and full_scan_threshold:10000 KB. Filterable HNSW adds payload-based edges, ACORN (v1.16.0) explores second-hop neighbors, enable_hnsw=false (v1.17.0) suppresses extra edges, and a rebuild can be forced by incrementing ef_construct. Inference: the page presents these as tunables but reports no recall or latency measurement.
Source claim (L2087-L2285): sparse vector indexes are exact, combine mutable and immutable forms, support pinned/cached/cold tiers and dot-product only, and need no predefined vector size.

Source claim (L2286-L2391): IDF (v1.10.0) is enabled by a modifier and computed per shard with the stated formula; per-tenant scoping uses the idf search parameter. Inference: the formula and shard scope describe a query-time statistic, not an index-time precomputation.

notes: Source claim (lines 1-4): title 'The Hexagonal (Ports & Adapters) Architecture', HaT Technical Report 2005.02 dated 2005-09-04 (v0.9, to be updated after reader comments), author Alistair Cockburn, and abstract: create the application without a UI or database so automated regression tests can run, it works when the database is unavailable, and applications can be linked without user involvement.

Source claim (lines 5-10): pattern 'Ports and Adapters (Object Structural)', alternative name 'Hexagonal Architecture'; intent is equal driving by users, programs, tests or batch scripts and isolated development/testing; adapters convert external events into procedure calls/messages and the application is ignorant of input-device nature; Figure 1 is a raster diagram.

Source claim (lines 11-16): motivation is business-logic infiltration into UI code, which blocks automated testing, batch operation and programmatic driving; adding a new layer fails without a mechanism to detect violations; the same coupling problem exists on the database side, and the article says the two problems are symmetric.

Source claim (lines 17-30): the solution exploits inside/outside asymmetry rather than left/right; inside code should not leak outside; ports are purposeful conversations defined by an API, with technology-specific adapters; many applications have only two ports, but the hexagon is not about six - it provides drawing room for two, three or four ports; port/adapter naming reflects these purposes.

Source claim (lines 31-39): Figure 2 shows two active ports and several adapters each; Figure 3 maps the same application to three layers and numbers a four-stage development sequence: FIT with a constant-as-mock rate, add GUI, integration testing against a real test DB, then live use.

Source claim (lines 40-71): sample code is a discount application (discount(amount)=amount*rate(amount)) with amount from the user and rate from a database; Stage 1 uses FIT's ColumnFixture with a constant rate, an HTML test table, and a command-line FIT runner.

Source claim (lines 72-92): Stage 2 adds a UI adapter; Stage 3 introduces RateRepository, RepositoryFactory and MockRateRepository, updates Discounter to accept a repository, and concludes that this is the simplest version of the architecture.

Source claim (lines 93-109): Application Notes distinguish primary/driving from secondary/driven ports; FIT is the natural primary test adapter and mocks the secondary one; use cases should be written at the application boundary; port count is a matter of taste, with examples of four, four and three natural ports.

Source claim (lines 110-132): Known Uses include a weather-alert system with four ports, API-drivable Mac/Windows applications, web APIs such as Google Maps and Flickr, stored-output and stereo-system examples; distributed large-team development and separated UI/application development are explicitly still trial uses and not counted as established uses.

Source claim (lines 133-147): Related Patterns compare ports-and-adapters with the generic Adapter pattern, MVC (primary ports only), mock objects and Loopback, Pedestal, Checks, and Dependency Inversion/Injection including Spring configuration.

Source claim (lines 148-159): Acknowledgements credit Gyan Sharma for the sample code and Rebecca Wirfs-Brock, Ward's wiki and Kevin Rutherfold; References list FIT, Adapter, Pedestal, Checks, Dependency Inversion, Dependency Injection, Mock Object, Loopback and use cases.

sections.heading: Speaking in POJO instead of ByteBuf

notes: Source claim: the page is titled 'Netty.docs: User guide for 4.x' and opens by saying it is automatically generated from a GitHub Wiki page; its last line reads 'Last retrieved on 06-Oct-2026' (L0-L4, L452).
Source claim: the guide's only stated run prerequisites are 'the latest version of Netty and JDK 1.6 or above' (L19); the body names no 4.x patch release, and the title is major-version scoped.

Source claim: Preface distinguishes general-purpose protocols from special-purpose implementations and names legacy proprietary-protocol interoperability as a motivating case (L6-L9); The Solution describes Netty as an asynchronous event-driven NIO client/server framework for TCP/UDP protocol servers and clients (L10-L14).

Source claim: DiscardServerHandler extends ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter; the prose says ByteBuf is reference-counted and the handler is responsible for release(), showing a try/finally ReferenceCountUtil.release(msg) pattern (L31-L55).

Source claim: the DiscardServer bootstrap creates 'boss' and 'worker' NioEventLoopGroup instances, uses ServerBootstrap with NioServerSocketChannel and a ChannelInitializer, sets SO_BACKLOG and SO_KEEPALIVE, binds, and shuts both groups down with shutdownGracefully() in finally (L75-L114).

Source claim: the guide says event-loop thread count and Channel-to-thread mapping depend on the EventLoopGroup implementation and may be constructor-configurable, and distinguishes option() (parent ServerChannel) from childOption() (accepted Channels) (L108-L113).

Source claim: the TIME server allocates a 4-byte ByteBuf with ctx.alloc().buffer(4), writeAndFlush()es a 32-bit time and closes in a ChannelFutureListener; the prose contrasts ByteBuf reader/writer indices with java.nio.ByteBuffer.flip() (L154-L184).

Source claim: the stream-based transport section says TCP is a queue of bytes rather than packets, so receivers must deframe; it shows a cumulative-buffer fix and then ByteToMessageDecoder/ReplayingDecoder with decode() adding zero or more messages (L248-L322).

Source claim: the POJO section defines UnixTime, moves extraction into a decoder, adds a ChannelOutboundHandler encoder and MessageToByteEncoder, and notes passing the original ChannelPromise through while leaving flush to a separate handler (L326-L390).

Source claim: Summary calls the page a 'quick tour' and points to the io.netty.example package and upcoming chapters; Shutting Down says shutdownGracefully() returns a Future that completes when the group and its Channels terminate (L391-L396).

sections.heading: 3. Specifying Replicated Data Types and Stores
4. Store Semantics and Data Type Correctness
A. Additional proofs of data type correctness
B. Additional material on replication-aware simulations (B.1-B.3)
D. Additional material on consistency axioms (D.1-D.4)

notes: Source claim: title and authors are 'Replicated Data Types: Specification, Verification, Optimality' by Sebastian Burckhardt, Alexey Gotsman, Hongseok Yang and Marek Zawirski; the first page identifies POPL '14, 22-24 January 2014, San Diego, DOI 10.1145/2535838.2535848 and ACM copyright 2014 (L0-L8, L51-L60).

Source claim: the abstract proposes relations over events for specifying replicated data types and replication-aware simulations for verification; it reports 7 existing implementations of 4 data types (LWW register, counter, multi-value register, observed-remove set), lower bounds proving 4 implementations optimal, and axiomatic multi-object consistency (L9-L31).

Source claim: §1 frames CAP as making strong consistency incompatible with availability under partitions, calls 'eventual consistency' a catch-all, and motivates conflict resolution with zip-code, shopping-cart and post/comment anomalies (L37-L131).

Source claim: §2 defines an implementation as (Σ, σ0, M, do, send, receive), separates op-based from state-based designs, and gives op-based counter, state-based counter and state-based LWW register (Def. 1, Fig. 2; L218-L390).

Source claim: abstract executions are (E, repl, obj, oper, rval, ro, vis, ar) with ro total per replica, vis acyclic and ar total per object (Def. 2); operation contexts and Fτ determine return values (Defs. 3-5; L397-L548).

Source claim: counter reads count visible inc events; LWW returns the sequential result of ar-ordered visible operations; multi-value register returns visible writes not superseded in vis; observed-remove set returns adds not removed by a visible remove (L549-L657).

Source claim: concrete executions and Fig. 3 define do/send/receive transitions; transport specifications such as T-Unique restrict delivery; Vstate is (ro ∪ del)+ restricted to do events, while Vop adds replica-order/delivery paths with a no-intervening-send condition; correctness is Def. 7 sat[V,T] (L658-L857).

Source claim: replication-aware simulations relate object states and messages to instrumented abstract executions through INIT, DO, SEND and RECEIVE (Def. 8/Fig. 5); Theorem 9 proves soundness and Theorem 10 covers the state-based instantiation (L858-L1305).

Source claim: §6 measures worst-case metadata overhead, uses experiment families and Lemma 14 to prove Ω(n) for the state-based counter (Theorem 15) and Ω(n lg m) for the observed-remove set (Theorem 17); Fig. 10 lists matching bounds for the four data types (L1306-L1705).

Source claim: §7 defines store correctness against data-type specifications and axioms EVENTUAL, THINAIR, POCV, POCA, COCV and COCA; §D proves transport/axiom correspondences and that POCV is equivalent to RYW+MR+WFRV+MWV and POCA to WFRA+MWA (Prop. 37), plus the C/C++ shared-memory correspondence (Prop. 41; L1706-L1906, L6533-L7159).

Source claim: Appendix A proves optimized and original OR-set and multi-value register correctness; Appendix B proves Theorems 9-10 and the op-based instantiation (Theorem 23); Appendix C gives lower/upper space bounds (Theorems 24-35); Appendix D covers session guarantees, quiescent consistency and the C/C++ comparison (L2071-L7159).

The text layer splits sub/superscripts, relation arrows and operators across lines and preserves hyphenated breaks; figures and table layouts were not visually interpreted.

Candidate anchor for the offline-collaboration evidence note: this complete read covers §§3-9 and Appendices A-D, so the page's stated introductory-section inspection limit can be re-checked against the full specification, correctness, optimality and consistency-axiom material.

Candidate anchor for visibility, arbitration and causality: the paper's abstract executions use ro, vis and ar, define hb/hbo, and compare the LWW-register specialization with weak shared-memory models; Lamport clocks and vector clocks appear in the implementations and proofs.
Candidate anchor for §D.2 session guarantees: the paper axiomatizes RYW, MR, WFRV, WFRA, MWV and MWA and proves POCV equivalent to RYW+MR+WFRV+MWV and POCA to WFRA+MWA (Prop. 37).

Candidate anchor for the replication-model boundary: the paper assumes asynchronous message passing, possible loss/reordering/duplication and eventual consistency, not quorum consensus; its T-Unique, Vstate and Vop assumptions can be checked against this page's quorum and leader-change scope.

Candidate anchor for agreement versus consistency: the paper separates per-object data-type specifications from store-level consistency axioms and compares the LWW-register specialization with the C/C++ memory model, not with consensus agreement.
